activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA calls 4 to 60 degrees Celsius (40 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit) the danger zone, the range where bacteria in food multiply rapidly.
story:
Oliver wiped down the prep station at Marconi's, the restaurant where he'd been washing dishes since September, and watched Mr. Tremblay write the week's specials on the clippered sheet that hung by the walk-in. It looked like a puzzle: chicken Monday, fish Tuesday, the roasted vegetables whenever they fit. Mr. Tremblay cooked in batches on Sundays so the whole week ran smooth, and Oliver, who at sixteen had never planned a meal further ahead than tonight, wanted to learn how. His mother had started working nights at the hospital, and someone had to feed the house.

"That's the whole trick," Mr. Tremblay said, tapping the sheet. "One shopping list, one afternoon of cooking, seven dinners. You plan, you buy, you cook it all at once, then you reheat." He handed Oliver a stub of pencil. "Write down what you'd make."

Oliver wrote chili, because chili was cheap and his friend Karsen would eat anything with enough cumin in it. Karsen and Jayden had started coming by after school ever since Oliver's kitchen became the only one on the block where somebody was actually cooking. Oliver remembered his father, two years gone now, standing in that same kitchen on a Sunday, browning ground beef in the good pan, saying make enough for the whole week, buddy. His father had died in the spring, and Oliver had not cooked anything since, until this job, until now.

He made his list. He did the shopping on Saturday with Jayden, who carried the basket and read labels aloud like a game show host, and on Sunday Oliver browned the beef, softened the onions until they went glassy, opened the cans with the can opener that still had his father's fingerprints somewhere on it, probably. He simmered the pot for two hours, ladled out a bowl for Karsen, who had appeared at the door drawn by the smell, and put the rest aside to cool before refrigeration. Then Karsen put on a movie, and Jayden arrived with chips, and at some point past midnight Oliver fell asleep on the couch with the textbook for his biology unit open on his chest.

Karsen found the pot in the morning, still sitting on the stove, lid on, the kitchen cold and quiet. He stood over it a long time. He hadn't wanted to move it, in case moving it was somehow worse than leaving it, and he hadn't wanted to wake Oliver, who was still asleep with his face pressed into a couch cushion. So Karsen texted Jayden, and Jayden biked over, and by the time Oliver woke there were two friends in his kitchen arguing softly about a pot of chili.

"It's fine," Oliver said. "It's got a lid on it."

"You left it out all night," Karsen said. "That can't be fine."

Oliver got out his phone. In biology they had just done a unit on food safety and he'd half listened, so now he searched, and the numbers came up immediately, transfixing him for a moment with their precision: 4 to 60 degrees Celsius, 40 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit, the range where bacteria in food multiply rapidly. "The USDA calls that the danger zone," he read aloud. "That's the whole fact. Room temperature is right in the middle of it." He looked at the pot, then at his friends. He thought of his teacher's careful distinction between the etiology of a disease and its symptoms, the difference between where a thing starts and what you can see of it. Where this started was a covered pot sitting in the danger zone all night, and no argument about the lid changed that. "It's not tenable," he said. "I can't tell myself it's okay. I don't have the evidence."

"So we throw it out," Jayden said, already reaching for the pot handles.

They carried it to the sink and poured it out, all of it, the onions Oliver had softened one by one, the beef he'd browned in his father's pan. Karsen washed the pot without being asked. Jayden, who had a twenty in his sock for reasons he never explained, put it on the counter and said, "Soup. Tonight. My treat. You cook, we'll do the dishes."

That Sunday Oliver tried again, and this time he stayed awake. He spread the chili into shallow pans so it would cool fast, moved them into the fridge, and set an alarm on his phone for every twenty minutes until the pans stopped steaming. When Mr. Tremblay asked him on Monday how the week had gone, Oliver said he'd poisoned no one, which Mr. Tremblay seemed to consider high praise. He'd made a plan, he'd broken it, and he'd fixed the break in the plan rather than the story about the plan, and he still wasn't sure which of those mattered more.

The following Sunday, Karsen showed up at the door carrying onions in a paper bag. "I figured we'd double the batch," he said, "and this time we take shifts staying up."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer, being in an offside position is not an offence by itself; a player is penalized only when involved in active play, and there is no offside from a throw-in, goal kick or corner.
story:
The television at Grandpa Ray's house was older than Hunter was, with a color balance that made every pitch look faintly like key lime pie, and for the final it had drawn a congregation: two uncles, a cousin, Cruz, Davis, and Ms. Nielsen from next door, who had brought a bowl of pretzels and opinions on everything except soccer. Hunter had the good armchair, the one by the window, and he was defending it with his legs.

"CORNER," bellowed Uncle Marcus, as though the referee might hear him from three time zones away. "Why are they wasting a corner, nobody ever scores from those."

"Ronaldo scores from those," said Davis, without looking up from the plate he was systematically clearing like a man at his last meal on earth. Davis had absconded with the last pretzel half an hour ago and shown no remorse.

The taker rolled the ball slightly with his palm, backed up, and whipped it toward the near post, where a striker in blue had been standing, frankly, in a very suspicious location. The ball glanced off his head and bulged the net. The room detonuted. Grandpa Ray's coffee table survived on a technicality.

"OFFSIDE!" Uncle Marcus was on his feet, pointing at the screen with a remote control, which lent the accusation an official air. "He was standing behind the whole line, that's offside, that's offside all day long. The ref's been bought. Parasitism, that's what that is, the whole league's got it."

Hunter shifted forward. He had played center back for four years under a coach who had drilled one lesson into him with the patience of erosion: standing in an offside position wasn't an offence by itself. You were only penalized if you became involved in active play, and there was no offside at all from a throw-in, a goal kick, or a corner. He'd learned it the humiliating way, actually, in a flashback that visited him now whether he wanted it or not: fifteen years old, league semifinal, Hunter's entire defensive line had stepped up together with the synchronized smugness of boys who had read exactly one paragraph about the game, and the other team's winger had simply stood still behind them like a man waiting for a bus, not offside, because the ball hadn't gone anywhere yet, and the moment his teammate played it forward and he chased it down and scored, the flag came up, and the coach had said, "He wasn't offside until he got involved, and then he was," and Hunter had spent the next week feeling like the universe had fine print everywhere.

"It was a corner," Hunter said. His voice came out smaller than the sentence deserved.

"What?"

"It came straight from the corner. There's no offside from a corner." He tried to keep the coach's voice out of his own. "Or a goal kick, or a throw-in. And even apart from that, standing in an offside position isn't the offence. You only get penalized when you get involved in the play."

Uncle Marcus looked at Hunter, then at the screen, where the referee was signaling the goal with the serene indifference of a man being shouted at through a television. The VAR check came and went in an interminable ninety seconds of the striker standing in freeze-frame, offside-positioned as anything, being conclusively not offside.

"See, he was standing right there," Marcus said, jabbing the remote again.

"He was," Hunter agreed. "That's allowed. That's the whole thing. He can stand there all day. It only matters when he gets active, and from a corner it doesn't even matter then."

"So the rules reward lurking," said Ms. Nielsen, who had been quiet in the way of someone composing a thesis. "A whole legal framework for standing somewhere ominous until the last possible second. I like this sport better than I expected."

"Wait," said Cruz, who had been following the argument the way one follows a tennis rally. "So in the semifinal, when you told us their guy was offside the whole second half and Davis called you paranoid, was he actually offside?"

"No," Hunter said. "He was in an offside position. Every time the ball came near him he got involved and then the flag went up, but in between, he was just standing there. Legal. Davis called me paranoid anyway."

"I stand by it," said Davis, crumbs falling from his chin like evidence. "You were paranoid. You were also right. Those aren't mutually exclusive, that's your whole personality."

Marcus sank back into the couch with the deflation of a man whose injustice had been repossessed by fine print. On the screen, the replay came around again, and this time the whole room watched it differently, even Grandpa Ray, who until now had been pretending to follow the game while actually watching the family. The striker stood stock still in his ominous acre of grass, the ball curved in, and only at the last instant did the man move, and it was the movement, Hunter understood, the becoming involved, that had ever been against the rules, not the standing, not the waiting, not any of the long patient parts.

"So the flag," Cruz said slowly, "isn't about where you are. It's about when you act."

"It's about both," Hunter said. "I think." He considered the goal on the screen, considered his semifinal, considered how much of the game he had played by feel and how recently the feel had acquired sentences. "Honestly, I'm still not sure I could call it live, at speed. But I know it wasn't offside, and I know Marcus got robbed of nothing."

"I got robbed of a grievance," Marcus said. "Those are the expensive kind."

Ms. Nielsen leaned over and refilled the pretzel bowl, and the clock started again, and in the sixty-third minute somebody's winger, level with the last defender, timed his run so finely that when the flag stayed down and he scored, the entire room turned to Hunter at once.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Alyssa arrived at the ice cream shop eleven minutes early, which she decided to think of as seven minutes early plus four minutes of useful reconnaissance. Through the window she could see the whole layout: the freezer case along the back wall, the counter with its laminated menu curling at the corners, and a chalkboard that said TODAY'S QUIRK: BALSAMIC STRAWBERRY in someone's hopeful handwriting. Ms. Menon from two doors down was already installed at the corner table with a book and a small dish of something plain, a woman whose ice cream choices had the discipline of an ascetic: one scoop, dark chocolate, no toppings, no ceremony.

Alyssa ordered a single scoop of pistachio, because pistachio sounded like a decision made by someone composed, and took the table nearest the window. She had rehearsed the first thirty seconds of the date so many times that she half believed they had already happened, which was the problem with being cerebral about things: you could exhaust an experience before it began. At 4:03, Harry came through the door shaking rain off his jacket, and the rehearsed version dissolved instantly, because in none of her rehearsals had he been damp.

"You got pistachio," he said, sliding into the chair across from her. "That's a serious flavor. That's a flavor with opinions."

"It's a flavor that knows what it wants," she said, and was pleased with herself for about a second and a half before she started worrying that pistachio-knowledge was not, in fact, a personality.

He ordered the balsamic strawberry, purely out of loyalty to the chalkboard, and spent the first spoonful making a face that he tried to suture over with a compliment, so that what came out was "it's interesting," delivered with the strained sincerity of someone lying to a hostess. Alyssa laughed before she could stop herself, and he laughed too, and for a while it was fine. They talked about the physics teacher who lectured to the clock and never to the room, and about whether sea creatures knew they were wet, and about Jonah's party, which they had both attended from opposite corners without speaking, a fact they had apparently been saving.

Then came the silence. Not a long one; eight seconds, maybe ten. Alyssa filled it by describing her summer plans in more detail than any sixteen-year-old's summer could sustain, and somewhere in the middle of the municipal swimming schedule she heard her own voice as if from a great distance and stopped talking. Harry was nodding. He was being polite. He was calculating the earliest exit that decency would permit. She knew the math because she was doing it from the other side, and it was almost a relief to have something to be good at.

When they finished, he paid for both of them even though she reached for her wallet, and they stood outside under the awning while the rain decided what it wanted to do. "This was good," he said. "We should, like, do it again sometime."

"Sure," she said, in the tone people use for sure, the tone that commits to nothing and could be deployed to a door-to-door salesman with a clear conscience. He walked east. She walked west. She was two blocks from home before she let the replay begin.

It opened with the pistachio, obviously, and moved through the swimming schedule at merciless length. Every silence she had let fall, every joke he hadn't laughed hard enough at, the moment she had knocked the napkin dispenser and caught it in a way that was somehow worse than dropping it. By the time she reached her street she had assembled a complete case, and the verdict was obvious: he had endured her. The word endure arrived unbidden and settled in like a tenant.

She stood on her own front steps rather than going in, because her mother would ask how it went and Alyssa did not yet have a version of the truth that was survivable. She took out her phone, not to text anyone, just to hold something. Jonah had sent a message to the group chat an hour ago, a screenshot from some psychology site with the caption "harry's in his lab era??" The screenshot was about a 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues, and it said that after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. There was a name for it, the article said, and Jonah had underlined the name: the liking gap.

Alyssa read it twice on the steps. It did not tell her Harry had enjoyed her company; she understood that much. It told her something narrower and stranger, that her own accounting was probably the least reliable document in the case file. She thought about how he had laughed at the balsamic strawberry face before she had even finished making it, and about the fact that he had brought up the party, unprompted, from his corner to hers. She thought about how she would be home replaying this exact stretch of pavement, and how he might be doing the same thing in the other direction, both of them composing verdicts on evidence that pointed somewhere else.

It stayed uncertain, she conceded, standing there while the rain finally committed. Maybe he had endured her. Maybe the study was about strangers in labs and had nothing to do with a damp boy and a girl with a serious flavor. But the possibility had shifted sides, and it took her side with it.

She typed "today was good, we should do it again" and read it once, deleted "good," put "good" back, and pressed send before the replay could reopen for cross-examination. Then she went inside, and from the kitchen her mother called, "So?" and Alyssa, taking off her wet shoes, said, "We're getting ice cream again next Saturday."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Galileo showed that the path of a projectile, ignoring air resistance, is a parabola, in his book Two New Sciences, published in 1638.
story:
The skate park emptied toward evening until only James, Drayden, and the sound of wheels on concrete remained. James sat on the lip of the bowl with a physics worksheet on his knee, watching Drayden launch off the quarter pipe again and again. The problem on the page involved a stone thrown at some angle, and the textbook wanted two things at once: how far it went and how high it rose. James had circled the given velocity three times, as if circling it harder would make it confess. What he could not see was how the same number could govern two different motions, sideways and up, at the same time.

"You're doing homework here," Drayden said, rolling to a stop in front of him. Drayden had that way of making a statement into a question without changing anything but his eyebrows.

"It's due Monday," James said. "Watch, though. Do that jump again." Drayden dropped in without arguing, pumped once, and rose off the coping, board tucked under him. James tracked him with his eyes the whole way up and the whole way down, and what he noticed, for the first time, was the shape. Not a line, not an arc like a doorway. A curve that rose steeply, eased, hung for a half second, and steepened again on the way down. He had drawn that curve in math class all last semester, plotted it point by point, and its name surfaced before he could stop it. "Parabola," he said, mostly to himself.

He flipped through the textbook's chapter, past the practice problems, and found a shaded box in the margin, the kind teachers said you could skip. Galileo, it said, had shown that the path of a projectile, ignoring air resistance, is a parabola. The result appeared in his book Two New Sciences, published in 1638. James read the sentence twice. He looked up at Drayden, mid-air again, and the two things overlaid each other, the printed sentence and the boy against the sky, like two transparencies held to the light. A dead Italian and a Tuesday evening at the skate park, and the same curve.

Drayden rolled up beside him, cheeks red, and looked over his shoulder at the page. "What are you grinning at?"

"Nothing, it's just, you keep making that shape when you jump. Somebody figured that out four hundred years ago." He tapped the margin box. "Galileo showed that a projectile's path, ignoring air resistance, is a parabola. Two New Sciences, 1638."

"Did he skateboard?"

"Ramp, no gravity, basically the same thing," James said, and Drayden laughed and drank from his water bottle, and the water that missed his mouth fell in a thin curved stream, and James watched even that, wondering whether it fell the same way, whether the curve held for spilled water or only for stones and skaters. He did not know. The book said ignoring air resistance, and the world was mostly air resistance.

From where Drayden stood, gulping water, James looked different than usual, hunched over the book with his pencil moving, but also talking too fast, pointing at the ramp, at the bottle, at the page, as if all three were connected by something invisible. Drayden had known James since seventh grade and had watched him fail units before, this same hunched posture with none of the pointing. He sat down on the concrete beside him. "Show me the problem," he said, mostly because it seemed wrong to leave him alone with whatever was happening.

"The thing is," James said, drawing on the back of the worksheet, "I keep trying to use the whole speed at once. But if the path is this curve, then maybe sideways and up are separate. Sideways nothing slows it down, if you ignore air. Up, gravity pulls it. So the sideways part stays the same the whole flight, and the up part changes, and together they make the parabola." He drew a horizontal arrow, a vertical arrow, then the curve between them. Was that actually why it was a parabola, or was that just a picture that felt right? The margin box had not said, and he was honest enough with himself to admit the drawing might be a guess wearing the costume of an answer. But when he split the velocity into components with trigonometry and worked the numbers, the stone landed where the book said it would, and he sat very still with that.

"Did you get it?" Drayden asked.

"I got the answer," James said. "Whether I got it got it, I don't know yet."

"That's more thinking than my whole week," Drayden said. He stood, stepped onto his board, and pushed off toward the quarter pipe. At the coping he crouched, rose, and hung for an instant against the pale sky, and James, without meaning to, traced the curve in the air with his pencil, following him down.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: The 17th edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, published in 2017, began discouraging 'ibid.' in favor of shortened citations that repeat the author and a short title.
story:
Ava spread her draft across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighting the corners with salt shakers because the window was open and the lake wind came through the screen like it had somewhere to be. The paper was supposed to argue something, actually argue it, with footnotes and a bibliography in Chicago style, and Mr. Cho had handed it back with a red circle around the fourth page and one word in the margin: outdated.

"Outdated how?" her grandmother said, setting down two mugs of coffee neither of them would finish. She went to the bookshelf without waiting for an answer, the shelf above the radio where the dictionaries lived, and came back with a style guide so old its cover had gone the color of weak tea. "Here. This got me through college. Everything you need is in there."

Ava opened it beside her marked-up draft. The old book was firm on the point: after a first full citation, you could repeat the source with the single word ibid., short and tidy, Latin, meaning "in the same place." Mr. Cho's circle sat around exactly that word, three times on one page, like a fence around something dangerous.

"So he's wrong and the book's right," her grandmother said, tapping the page. "Or he's right and the book's wrong. One of them has to give."

"It doesn't work like that anymore, I think." Ava pulled out her phone and typed fast, and there it was, which was almost worse than not finding it. The 17th edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, published in 2017, had started discouraging ibid. in favor of shortened citations, the author's name and a short title repeated each time. Her grandmother's book predated the change by decades. Mr. Cho's red circle was not an insult; it was a correction from the future. "The new edition came out in 2017. They don't want ibid. anymore. You just repeat the author and a short title."

Her grandmother sat back down slowly, the way she did when the news was about a person. "I used that word in every paper I wrote," she said. "Four years of ibid."

"You were the oligarchy of ibid," Ava said. "You and everyone from your generation, just ruling over the footnote."

Her grandmother laughed, then stopped laughing fairly quickly, and Ava wished she could cauterize the joke, seal it off before it touched the real thing underneath, which was that the book on the table was something her grandmother had carried from apartment to apartment for fifty years and now it was simply, factually, wrong about its own subject. "You know my thesis is about the Revision Committee," Ava said, quieter now, "how they said they were protecting tradition and really they were protecting their own interests. It's specious, the whole argument they made, it sounds reasonable until you check the numbers. And I've been sitting here defending a tradition all afternoon because it was yours."

"So change my mind for me," her grandmother said. "That's the assignment, isn't it. Argue something."

Ava took a fresh page and started rebuilding the fourth footnote, the shortened form, author and short title, and then the fifth, and the sixth, and by the seventh her grandmother had taken the old book into her lap and was following along with one finger, learning the new rules from Ava's page the way she had once learned the old ones from a professor whose name she still said with a certain tilt of her head. Outside, a boat horn sounded twice, some neighbor calling a dog in off the dock. Somewhere in the middle of it Ava found she could not remember which of them had originally argued for the book.

"There," she said at last, and turned the draft around on the table. Her grandmother read the footnotes down the margin, all the little repeated authors and short titles, and put her hand flat on the old guide's cover, not quite closing it.

"I'll keep it anyway," her grandmother said. "For the spine if nothing else." She smoothed the draft's curled corner with her thumb and pushed it back across the table. "And you'll put my name in the acknowledgments when Mr. Cho gives you an A."

"When," Ava said.

"If," her grandmother said, and stood to rinse the mugs, and left the old book lying open on the table to the page with ibid., faceup in the wind from the lake.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: Ontario combines the federal GST with its provincial sales tax into a single 13 percent Harmonized Sales Tax, shown as one HST line on receipts.
story:
The paycheque lay on the kitchen table like a small accusation. Ashton had worked thirty-one hours at the greenhouse over the past two weeks, stacking trays and hauling soil, and he had done the arithmetic in his head all week: thirty-one hours at sixteen dollars an hour, four hundred ninety-six dollars, which meant the drum kit Celia was selling for four hundred was finally within reach. The number on the cheque said four hundred twelve and change. He read the stub twice, then a third time, as though the missing eighty-four dollars might surface if he stared hard enough.

"So where'd it go?" Celia had asked him at school that morning, when he'd told her the total with the wary tone of someone reporting a theft. She wanted the sale, he knew that. She'd been trying to get rid of the kit since March, saving for something she wouldn't name, and every week he didn't buy it was a week she stayed four hundred dollars further from whatever it was. She'd even offered to hold it for him. "Ask someone who's actually been paid before."

His mother was at the sink now, peeling carrots, and he slid the stub across the table toward her. She dried her hands and sat down opposite him. She didn't take it from him, which was her way; she read it where it lay.

"Income tax," she said, tapping one line. "Federal and Ontario both take a cut. And that one's Canada Pension Plan, that one's employment insurance. Deductions, they call them." She said the word casually, the way she said words like escrow and amortize, terms she seemed to have absorbed from some aquifer of adult knowledge he had never found the wellhead of. "You'll get some of the tax back when you file your return, probably. You don't earn enough for them to keep it all."

"So the four hundred twelve is real, though. That's mine."

"That's yours," she said, and went back to the carrots.

He did the arithmetic again, and then a third kind of arithmetic occurred to him, the kind he'd been avoiding. The kit was four hundred, but that wasn't the whole cost, was it. He'd bought a coffee and a sandwich at the place near the greenhouse yesterday, and he pulled the receipt out of his jacket pocket now and smoothed it on the table beside the paycheque, the two documents side by side like pieces of evidence in a case he was building against his own budget. The receipt listed the sandwich, the coffee, and then a single line, HST, a little under a dollar and a half.

One tax line. He frowned at it. In the movies, in older books, there were always two taxes, provincial and federal, stacked separately. He'd half expected to see both here, itemized like the deductions on his stub. Instead there was just the one. He turned the receipt over. Nothing on the back but a survey link.

Ariella had come over to drop off the biology notes he'd missed, and now she sat across from him eating cereal at four in the afternoon, which she considered a normal thing to do. He pushed the receipt toward her.

"Why's there only one tax line?" he asked.

"Because Ontario combines the federal GST with the provincial sales tax into one thirteen percent Harmonized Sales Tax," she said, with her mouth full, as if this were the most obvious thing in the world. "It's just the HST. One line." She went back to her cereal. Ariella could recite the periodic table and every bus route in the east end but could not explain why she knew any of it; the information simply lived in her, mesmerizing in its totality, and she had long ago stopped being impressed by her own recall.

Thirteen percent. He took out his phone and multiplied. Four hundred dollars for the kit, times one point one three. Four hundred fifty-two. He sat back. He had four hundred twelve and a bus pass and eleven days until the next paycheque, and the gap between what he had and what the kit would actually cost at the register was forty dollars he had not planned for, because he had been thinking of prices as though they were the prices.

"They should teach this," he said. "They teach us the supply of water in Canada, they teach us the prolix tragedy of the Jesuit relations, nobody teaches you that the number on the tag is not the number you pay."

"They did teach it," Ariella said. "Grade eight. You were drawing on your binder, I remember."

He looked at the paycheque again, at the return his mother had mentioned, the possibility of money coming back, and then at the receipt, at money already gone. Two directions, one taking before he'd earned and giving some back later, one taking at the till with no return at all. He was honest enough with himself to admit he didn't fully understand where the lines were drawn, why the government trusted him with a refund but not with the original amount, why thirteen percent felt different coming off a paycheque than coming off a sandwich. What he did understand, for the first time, was that both of them were real, and that he'd been budgeting in a fantasy version of money.

He texted Celia. Can you do four hundred even, cash, no tax? It's a private sale, between us.

She replied within a minute, which for Celia was a confession of how badly she wanted it gone. It's a private sale, so no HST anyway. But I need four fifty, not four hundred. Sorry. I've been short all month.

He read it twice. So the kit had grown by fifty dollars, and his knowledge had grown by thirteen percent and a payroll stub's worth of deductions, and the two things didn't cancel out, they just sat there together, one problem and one small competence, side by side like the paycheque and the receipt still lying on the table.

He counted it out in his head one more time. Four twelve in hand. Eleven days to the next cheque, with more deductions, and a refund somewhere downstream that he'd have to file paperwork to claim. Ms. Chatterjee, his law teacher, had once said that most of adult life was learning the rules after you'd already broken them, and he'd thought she was being bleak. Now it seemed almost generous, like being handed a map after the detour instead of no map at all.

He typed: I can do four twenty-five on Friday, after I get paid. Four fifty in two weeks if you can wait. Then he set the phone face-down on the table, next to the receipt, and started peeling the carrots his mother had left on the counter.

The phone buzzed against the wood. He let it sit there while he finished the first one.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by communication researcher Jeffrey Hall estimated it takes roughly 50 hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
The U-Haul trailer thumped over the expansion joints, and Alexandra counted them out of habit the way she used to count sidewalk cracks on the walk to Gaelle's house. In the passenger seat she held her phone with the draft message open, a goodbye so long it had stopped meaning anything, forty lines about the parking lot behind the gym and the night Blair fell into the creek and the way the streetlight outside Gaelle's window buzzed in a specific key. She scrolled to the bottom and did not send it. Her mother drove with both hands on the wheel and the radio off, because for once she had agreed that silence was a reasonable passenger.

Three weeks of the new town were already behind them, in a sense, because Alexandra had gone ahead in June to register for classes while the movers packed. Three weeks of a school where she knew names but not people, where a girl named Renee saved her a seat in lab and Alexandra still couldn't have said whether that was friendship or logistics. She had written to Blair about it, and Blair, who was prolix in text the way some people are only in writing, had sent back a link with no comment except "read this, it's not as sad as it sounds."

The link was a study from 2018 by a communication researcher named Jeffrey Hall, and the number inside it had stuck to Alexandra like a burr: roughly fifty hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. Not fifty hours of longing, or of missing the old town, or of drafting messages in the car. Fifty hours of actual time. She read it twice at a rest stop in Ohio while her mother pumped gas, and then a third time, and then she looked at the draft on her phone and understood, with a small cold clarity, why it had been so hard to write. You could not compress a person into a paragraph. You could not sublimate Gaelle into an elegy and call it settled.

"Mom, can I ask you something weird?" she said, getting back in and pulling the door shut against the wind. "How long did it take you and Diane to become friends? Like actually friends, not neighbor friends."

Her mother laughed, checking the mirror before pulling out. "Honest answer? Years. We were polite for two years and then her basement flooded and I went over with the wet vac and we sat on her porch after and something changed." She glanced over. "Why?"

"Some researcher counted it. Fifty hours, more or less, to go from acquaintance to casual friend. I keep doing the math on the new school and it doesn't add up to anything yet, and I couldn't figure out if that meant something was wrong with me."

"Nothing's wrong with you," her mother said, too quickly, and Alexandra let it go, because the answer had the shape of reassurance rather than thought, and she was not in the market for that shape today.

In the driver's seat, her mother watched the road and did not say what she was thinking, which was that Alexandra had inherited from her exactly this habit, the need to measure a thing before trusting it. The draft message glowed on the girl's phone in her lap, and the mother remembered being seventeen and writing a letter like that to a girl named Priya, a letter she had eventually torn into confetti in a dormitory trash can because it had become, by its last page, a museum exhibit rather than a hello. There was a postcard stand at the next service plaza. She signaled early.

"We're stopping," she announced. "I need coffee and you need a postcard."

"Mom, I have a phone."

"Postcards are better. You have to choose what fits."

Alexandra bought one with a heron on it, absurdly, a heron for a girl who had never seen a heron, and stood at the counter while her mother paid for coffee. She deleted the draft, all forty lines, and felt no grief about it, only lightness, and in the lightness she noticed something she had not expected: the fifty hours ran in both directions. Gaelle had them already, banked, four years of parking lots and creek water. That was the thing the study couldn't measure and she couldn't either, whether banked hours stayed good, or whether distance quietly spent them down to nothing. She didn't know. Ms. Gallagher had told their English class that existentialism was mostly the insistence on choosing anyway, in the absence of guarantees, and Alexandra had rolled her eyes at the time, but here in the plaza with the heron card she thought maybe she finally saw what the woman had been pointing at.

She wrote on the back in blue ballpoint, small: "Fifty hours and you're still ahead. First one's on the new town when you visit." She underlined "visit," dropped the card in the mailbox by the door, and walked back to the car with her hands in her pockets, counting nothing.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: At a local maximum of a polynomial the derivative equals zero, because the tangent line at the top of the peak is horizontal.
story:
Jessica had spread her homework across the kitchen table by seven, though the house was still obstreperous with her little brother's music thudding through the wall, and she had already remonstrated with him twice through the door. The assignment was from Ms. Mercado's class: sketch the profit a student club could make selling sweatshirts, given some polynomial that rose, peaked, and fell away again. She was supposed to find the maximum, the price at which profit topped out, and she had no idea how.

She texted Adrienne first. Adrienne wrote back a single string of letters that might have been sympathy or might have been a yawn, and Jessica put the phone face-down and looked at the equation the way she looked at the physiology diagrams she had to memorize for another class, hoping that staring would make the parts resolve into a whole. It didn't. The graph in her textbook showed a smooth hill, and somewhere on top of that hill sat the answer, and the book kept saying the word derivative as though that explained anything.

Heath arrived at eight with his own worksheet and a bag of chips, because his mother had banished him until he finished the same assignment. "I asked my cousin," he said, dropping into the chair across from her. "He just kept saying slope, slope, like that was a whole speech."

Jessica pulled out a ruler and drew the curve freehand instead, big, taking up half a page. Then she leaned in close and drew short straight lines against the paper, trying to imagine what was happening to the curve at each point. On the way up the left side, her little line tilted steeply upward. Near the top it lay almost flat. Down the right side it tipped the other way. She sat back. "Look at this," she said. "Right at the peak, the line I'd draw is horizontal. Like the curve stops climbing before it starts falling."

Heath squinted at her sketch. "So the slope is zero at the top?"

"Maybe that's the whole thing," Jessica said. "The derivative is the slope, so at a maximum the derivative equals zero." She said it slowly, testing the weight of it. "So I don't have to guess where the top is. I set the derivative equal to zero and solve." She was already flipping back through her notes, through the rules for differentiating each term, her pencil moving faster than her certainty. Heath watched her work the algebra, which took two tries because she dropped a negative sign, and when she had a candidate number she plugged it back in and traced it on her sketch, and there it was, the exact price at the top of the hill.

"Wait," Heath said. "So for my problem too, the tangent line at the top of the peak is horizontal, so I just set my derivative to zero?" He had his own pencil out now. Jessica watched him copy her method without copying her arithmetic, which was sensible of him.

They worked in a quiet that even her brother seemed to respect, or maybe he had just gone to bed. Jessica finished her graph and then sat looking at it, and a question surfaced that she turned over without rushing. The slope went from positive to flat to negative, so the flat point marked a top, but what if a curve flattened somewhere that wasn't a top? She thought of the physiology unit again, how a heartbeat looks flat on a monitor for one instant between beats without being dead. Maybe a polynomial could do that too, pause on a slope without peaking. She said it out loud to Heath, and he frowned at his paper and said, "So zero means the top, except when it doesn't," and she laughed and wrote a note to ask Ms. Mercado in the morning, because she trusted the method more than she trusted her guess about its edges.

Adrienne texted again near ten: done, probably wrong, don't care. Jessica looked at her own finished page, at the hill with its flat instant marked in ink, and found she did care, which surprised her, because she had taken the class only because it fit her schedule. She had spent four years treating math as a thing to survive, and tonight it had behaved more like a set of doors, each one opening onto a question she hadn't thought to want answered.

Her mother came down for a glass of water and paused at the table. "You're still up?"

"Math," Jessica said, gathering Heath's chip bag into the trash.

"At this hour." Her mother said it in the tone of a woman building a case, but she was looking at the graph, at the careful straight line resting on the crest of the curve. "That looks almost pretty."

"It's a sweatshirt business," Jessica said. "We're at the top of the market." Heath snorted into his worksheet without looking up, and she pulled the page toward her again and added, in the margin, one more question for Ms. Mercado.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: The 'guidance hypothesis' from motor learning research holds that feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helps retention.
story:
Hannah arrived at the diamond early, before the eight-year-olds, and dragged the equipment bag to the pitcher's mound so she could see the whole field laid out in front of her. The problem she had been hired, more or less, to solve was the team's passing. The Tigers could hit, sort of, and they could catch when the ball came straight at their chests, but the moment a throw had to travel from shortstop to first base in a hurry, the ball went wide or high or into the dirt. She had three weeks and one notebook full of drills.

Her plan that first Tuesday was a triangle drill: three kids, ten feet apart, rotating throws while she stood at the center with her whistle. Every time a throw skipped off the grass, she stopped everything. Tuck the glove under the chin first. Point the front shoulder at the target. Follow through toward the base. She said these things so often that by the end of the hour the words had worn smooth, like coins rubbed between fingers.

Lewis came to watch, sitting backwards on the dugout bench with his bike helmet still on. "You talk more than my mom at a parent conference," he said, and she told him to shag foul balls if he was going to be useless. But she noticed something in the third practice, something she filed away without wanting to. When she stepped out to help a kid on the far side of the diamond, the throwing fell apart almost immediately, as though her voice had been holding their arms in the right positions and, absent it, the arms remembered nothing.

Saturday was the first game. Hannah stood by the fence with her notebook and watched a ground ball roll slowly toward her shortstop, a small boy named for a grandfather nobody had ever met. He fielded it cleanly. Then he looked up, and instead of throwing, he scanned the sideline, his eyes searching for her, and while he searched, the runner crossed the bag. In the fourth inning the second baseman turned a double play ball into a two-run overthrow, and after the game a small voice near the water bottles said, "You didn't tell me where to throw it."

She walked home the long way, past the public library, and sat in the baseball section with her notebook open and nothing written in it. She was not a person who gave up on her own system easily; she had spent a full Sunday building that system, and she suspected, with some justice, that she had confused effort with design. The coach of the high school varsity team, Ms. Nair, was there grading papers at a corner table, and when Hannah asked her outright how to fix throwing, Ms. Nair only smiled and slid a book across the table, one finger resting on a page before she gathered her things and left. Hannah read the page twice, and the phrase she carried out into the evening was one she'd never heard before, so she tested it on Lewis by phone that night, lying on her bedroom floor.

"It's called the guidance hypothesis," she said.

"Which means?"

"Feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it." She had copied the sentence down word for word, in the parsimonious way she took notes, nothing extra, no margin doodles. "Less frequent feedback helps retention. So I taught them to need me."

Lewis was quiet for a second, then said, "So stop talking," and she could hear him grinning, and she hung up on him without apology.

The next practice she ran the same triangle drill with one change, which was that she said nothing at all for the first ten throws. This was physically difficult. Every errant ball beseeched her, practically begged her for the little phrase that would fix it, and her mouth kept opening on instinct before she shut it. She let five throws go by, then gave one correction, then let five more pass in silence. The kids looked at her sideways at first, as if a vending machine had stopped working, and one girl asked whether Hannah was mad at them. Then, somewhere in the second rotation, the shortstop who had frozen in the game threw a bad ball, glanced toward the fence, found nothing there, and adjusted his own feet on the next throw without being told. It was not pretty. It was a start.

She kept the notebook but changed what went in it. Instead of a list of every mistake, she made a column for each kid and marked only every fifth throw, betting that a correction delivered rarely might outlast a correction delivered always, and that she would find out on Saturday whether the bet meant anything. There was a moment on Thursday when the whole plan seemed like an aphorism she had dressed up as a strategy, a tidy sentence masquerading as knowledge, and she wrote in the margin, maybe this only works for other people's teams, and then crossed it out because crossing out was also a kind of talking to herself she could not seem to quit.

The second game arrived under a flat gray sky. In the second inning a grounder hopped toward third, and Hannah stood at the fence with her hands jammed in her jacket pockets, saying nothing, though everything in her leaned forward. The third baseman fielded it. He looked up, and for one long second his eyes swept the sideline the way they had before, and Hannah held her breath, and Lewis, beside her now with his helmet still hooked on his handlebars, whispered, "Don't." The boy looked back at the bag. He planted his back foot, pointed his front shoulder at first, and threw.

The ball beat the runner by half a step. The first baseman held up his glove with the ball sitting in it like something found, and Hannah kept her hands in her pockets and said, to nobody, "Fifth one."

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: In the UK Parliament, a government bill's first reading is a formality: the bill is introduced without debate or a vote.
story:
The bus dropped them outside the mock legislature at nine, and by nine-thirty Victor's bill on school meal subsidies had already survived its first reading, which turned out to mean almost nothing. The clerk read the title aloud, entered it in the record, and moved on. Jaelyn, sitting beside him in the government benches, leaned over with a look of pure betrayal. "That was eleven seconds. We practiced for two weeks."

"First reading's a formality," Victor said. "It's introduced without a vote. There's no debate, nothing." He had read it in the procedure guide the night before, expecting it to matter somehow, and had decided not to tell anyone in case he was wrong. Now the emptiness of it spread through him like cold water. His bill, which he had drafted three times at his kitchen table, existed only as a line in a minute book.

"You could have warned us," Kayla whispered from the row behind. Her own bill, on bus fare caps, had suffered the same eleven-second fate, and she was taking it personally in a way that made Victor want to laugh and also want to apologize for the entire system. The Speaker called the chamber to order, and Ms. Kaminski, watching from the visitors' gallery with her arms folded, gave them all a small nod, as if to say the disappointment was part of the lesson. He resented the nod. He resented most things that came prepackaged as lessons.

The committee stage came after lunch, and there the bill stopped being a line and became an argument. A girl from the opposition benches, someone Victor had never spoken to despite four years of sharing a cafeteria, moved an amendment that would gut the subsidy by making it means-tested. She argued it with numbers, actual numbers, a printout of family income bands that she passed down the table like evidence at a trial. Victor had expected resistance but not competence. "Means-testing saves the program," she said. "Targeting the money where it's needed."

Jaelyn countered that means-testing carried a stigma, that the families who needed it most would be the least likely to apply, and that a universal benefit treated students with a baseline of dignity rather than suspicion. Victor listened to both of them and felt the strange sensation of agreeing with each in turn, the way you can see both sides of a valley only by standing exactly on the ridge between them. He had drafted the bill as universal because universal was cleaner, easier to defend, easier to believe in. Now the cleanliness looked less like principle and more like a congenital aversion to hard cases.

When his turn came to speak, he proposed a compromise: universal subsidy, but with a clause inviting a review after one year. "I can't tell you tonight whether targeting works better," he said, and the honesty landed strangely in the room, some students nodding, others shifting. "I can tell you we won't know unless we look." The amendment failed by four votes, which felt like a victory and also like the discovery that his own position had a hinge in it, a place where it could bend.

The debate in the full chamber lasted forty minutes, longer than anything Victor had ever spoken through. The opposition girl, whose name tag read only her riding and not her name, rose once more to say that a subsidy without limits was a blank cheque, and Kayla, in a gesture that dissolved whatever rivalry had been simmering between them since grade nine, stood to defend Victor's bill on the grounds that hungry students do not recuperate by lunchtime, that the afternoon is lost to them entirely. The vote came after the Speaker's bell, a ritual walk back into the chamber, and the ayes carried it by six.

The third reading, the assent, the Speaker's formula about the bill becoming law, all of it happened in under a minute. Victor stood when his bill was called and sat when it passed, and afterward Jaelyn found him by the coat rack. "So we spent a whole day," she said, "for it to be pretend."

"It's not pretend," Victor said, and then heard how sure he sounded, and softened it. "It's a rehearsal. That's different." He was already composing the letter he would write to the actual school board, one that would keep the universal clause and the review clause and admit, somewhere in the middle, that he had not made up his mind about the means test. Outside, the bus idled at the curb, and through its windows he could see Ms. Kaminski saving seats in the third row.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Earthenware pottery is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius, while porcelain is fired between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius.
story:
The kiln had sat in his grandfather's garage for eleven years, and Anthony had walked past it every summer without once touching it. This year was different, because this year he had a plan: two mugs, thrown at the community studio in town, glazed in the blue his grandfather used to keep on a shelf above the workbench, fired here so that the whole thing would be his. He had carried the greenware down the gravel drive in a shoebox padded with paper towels, holding it against his ribs the way you hold something you are afraid to want.

Zak came over on the second day, mostly to escape his own house, and stood in the doorway of the garage with his hands in his pockets. "You're actually doing this," he said. Not quite a question, not quite praise. With Zak, everything arrived as litotes, so Anthony had learned to take the understatement and add a layer himself. He set the shoebox on the bench and lifted out the first mug, a squat earthenware cylinder with his thumbprints wandering up one side like a path through arboreal country, dense and deliberate and slightly lost.

The second mug was not his. Arielle had thrown it at the studio the same evening, out of a bag of clay she had brought herself, pale gray and fine as flour, and she had handed it to him with the casualness of someone giving away almost nothing. "Fire it with yours," she had said. "It's porcelain." He had said sure. That was the whole conversation, and it had seemed, at the time, sufficient.

Ms. Mercer lived next door and had known his grandfather longer than Anthony had been alive. She came across the grass in the late afternoon carrying a plate of lemon bars, which was her way of checking on the house without saying she was checking on the house. She looked at the two mugs side by side on the bench, then at the kiln, and was quiet for a moment in a way that made Anthony quiet too. "Different kiln loads," she said finally, and set the plate down.

He did not understand her, and she did not elaborate, which was typical of everyone in this neighborhood and of this house especially. So he went looking. His grandfather's pottery notes were still in the cabinet under the workbench, three spiral notebooks with warped covers, and in the second one he found the page: firing schedules in his grandfather's cramped hand, a line for earthenware, a line for porcelain. Earthenware, below twelve hundred. Porcelain, twelve hundred to fourteen hundred. Underneath, in the margin, his grandfather had written temperatures, then crossed one out and written the lower one again, as if reminding himself twice.

Anthony sat on a paint can and read the page four times. The two mugs, sitting together on the bench like they belonged together, did not belong together. If he fired them in one load, one of them would be wrong. Either the earthenware would go too hot, or the porcelain would never go hot enough, and he understood without being told that this was not a matter of splitting the difference, because there was no temperature that suited both. He thought about calling Arielle, and his thumb was on her name before he stopped himself and put the phone face down on the bench.

Zak watched all of this from the doorway. "So run it twice," he said, when Anthony finally explained. Anthony looked at the kiln, which took hours to reach temperature and hours more to cool, and did the arithmetic of a Saturday and a Sunday, and of his mother arriving Sunday night to drive him home. "I can fire one," he said. "Maybe." He turned the shoebox over in his hands. His mug, the one with the wandering thumbprints. Arielle's, pale and fine, given away with a shrug.

He found himself defending each choice out loud, which was embarrassing, so he stopped. His was the project; that argument was clean. But hers was the gift, and a gift, he thought, carried an obligation to deliver it intact, and if he fired his own first, hers would wait two days in a garage in August heat, and unfired clay was not patient. He did not know which reasoning was the truer one. He knew only that he had to choose before the light went.

In the end he sequestered his own mug back in the shoebox, padding it again with the towels, and set Arielle's on the kiln shelf alone, centered and level, and switched on the elements. From the driveway, through the small square window of the garage door, the interior glowed a faint and steady orange, like a lamp left on in a room where someone was expected later.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but it acts mainly as a feedback: warmer air holds more water vapor, which amplifies warming started by other gases like carbon dioxide.
story:
Laurence stopped where the trail bent toward the overlook, not because her legs were tired but because Benson had asked a question she could not yet answer, and she had learned that questions like that were best faced standing still. Below them the water stretched flat and gray to the horizon, and a scattering of pelagic birds turned far out over it, riding some current she couldn't see. She had the printout folded in her jacket pocket, the graph Ms. Huang had handed out the day before, a single climbing line meant to be carbon dioxide across the last century.

"So say it back to me," Benson said. He walked a few steps ahead, then reversed, unable, as always, to hold still while thinking. "Tyrese is going to come at us with water vapor tomorrow. He told the whole team he found a website."

"And the website is right about one thing," Laurence said. "Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas. More of it in the air than carbon dioxide. If he says that part, he isn't lying."

Benson groaned and sat down on a root. "Then we lose. If water vapor is the biggest one, then carbon dioxide doesn't matter, and our whole case is garbage."

She took out the graph and sat beside him, smoothing it flat against her knee so the wind couldn't take it. The line rose in small sawtooth wiggles, up and down each year, but the trend underneath never once bent back down. She had spent an hour the night before trying to read it the way Ms. Huang had shown them, tracing the sawtooth with a fingertip until she could see the steeper climb hiding underneath the wiggles, the way you could stand in a crowd and still notice that the whole crowd was moving.

"Here's what I couldn't figure out at two in the morning," she said. "If water vapor is the biggest greenhouse gas, why does everyone care about this line instead? I kept thinking I was missing something huge." She paused, because admitting that still cost her something. She was the one who never missed things. In their history seminar she had once corrected Ms. Huang's dates on the board, and had spent a week afterward half proud and half ashamed, unable to decide which she should be. Ms. Huang had only said that historiography was an argument, not a settled list, and that being first to correct was worth less than being last to be sure.

"So what did you figure out?" Benson said.

"Tyrese explained it to me, actually. Last night, on the phone, after he sent me the website." She watched Benson's face change and kept going before he could interrupt. "He wasn't gloating. He genuinely wanted to know if he'd found a hole in our case, because if he had, he wanted it to be a real hole, not a cheap one. That's the thing about Tyrese." She looked out at the birds again, turning and turning on the invisible current. "Water vapor isn't the thing that starts the warming. It answers it. Warmer air holds more water vapor, and that extra water vapor amplifies the warming that other gases started. He said there's a word for that. Feedback."

Benson repeated the word slowly, as if tasting it. "So carbon dioxide pushes first, and water vapor follows and makes it worse."

"That's the shape of it," Laurence said, and then, because she had promised herself she would be honest even when it cost the team points, "though I can't yet tell you exactly how much of the graph is one and how much is the other. That part is still fuzzy for me. If someone asks tomorrow, I might say the wrong size of it." She had tried the night before to titrate her confidence, adding certainty in small measured amounts, and had stopped short of the point where certainty would have hardened into something false.

Benson stood up and held out his hand for the graph. He studied the climbing line for a long moment. "So when I rebut him, I don't deny what he found. I take it."

"You take it and you turn it," Laurence said. "That's better than denying it. He'll respect that more, honestly."

They walked on, faster now, the trail dropping toward the water through low pines. Laurence thought about how strange it was that Tyrese, their opponent, had handed them the center of their own case, and that she had almost not picked up the phone. Somewhere behind them the birds were still circling the same unseen thing.

"Run it once," Benson said. "I'm Tyrese. Water vapor is the real cause of warming, checkmate."

Laurence laughed, took a breath, and began.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: ProPublica, founded in 2007 as a nonprofit newsroom funded by donations, became the first online news source to win a Pulitzer Prize, in 2010.
story:
Charlie found the flyer taped to the library door on a Tuesday, right below the return slot: the advertisers' breakfast for The Clarion, the student paper she'd written for since sophomore year. Below that, in smaller print, a line about a new sponsor, Aldergate Fitness, whose owner sat on the school board.

She took the flyer inside and sat down across from Lilian at the long table by the windows, where the staff kept their laptops and their arguments. Lilian slid a spreadsheet toward her. "Coach says the paper loses money every month. Ads are the only way. Mr. Chaudhary already cashed the Aldergate cheque."

"Aldergate's owner votes on the school budget," Charlie said.

"So? It's an ad, not an article."

"It's a company whose interests run straight through this building."

Lilian folded her arms. "Then what do you want, bake sales?"

Charlie didn't answer. She turned to the terminal behind the reference desk and started searching, half for an argument, half for a way out. What she found surprised her enough that she printed it and carried it back to the table. "ProPublica," she said, tapping the page. "Founded in 2007. It's a nonprofit newsroom, funded by donations instead of ads. In 2010 it became the first online news source to win a Pulitzer Prize."

Maina looked up from layout. "Nobody owns it?"

"That's the idea. No owner, no advertiser to keep happy." Charlie felt the shape of an argument forming, something she could actually bring to the staff meeting on Friday. Donations, not ads. Independence instead of a sponsor whose name she'd have to keep out of a story.

That evening she drafted a proposal, trying to keep it pithy, the way their best editorials ran, but she kept writing around the thing she couldn't name: that money was money, and whoever gave it had hands. Her mother had inculcated that in her years ago, at the kitchen table, over envelopes from the bank: there is no free thing, only a thing whose cost you haven't been shown yet. Charlie deleted three paragraphs of certainty and settled on one paragraph of questions, which felt more honest and much weaker.

She texted Lilian a photo of the draft. Lilian's reply came as a message she read under her desk lamp, holding the phone close so her mother wouldn't see she was still awake. "Aldergate pulled out. Chaudhary says a donor stepped in instead. Anonymous. Meeting moved to Thursday."

At Thursday's meeting, fourteen people crowded the library's conference room. Mr. Chaudhary stood at the whiteboard, marker uncapped, and wrote DONOR in blue letters, then underlined it twice. "The money's real," he said. "Twice what Aldergate offered. The condition is that the donor stays unnamed."

"ProPublica publishes its donors," Charlie said, standing. "It has to, to keep its probity, its proof it can't be bought. If we take anonymous money, we've solved nothing. We've just hidden the owner."

"ProPublica is a national newsroom with lawyers," Chaudhary said. "We are a school paper with a photocopier."

"Then we publish nothing about the donor's interests and we say why, in print."

Maina cut in, voice flat. "The donor is the alumni association. I checked the cheque stub. It's their fund for student programs."

Lilian turned to Maina, then to Charlie, and there was a silence in which everyone did the arithmetic at once. The alumni association was the same group that had petitioned, twice, to cut the theatre budget and had called a Clarion story about that petition "divisive" in a letter to the principal.

"So the anonymous donor has interests too," Charlie said slowly, testing the sentence as she said it. "Not worse than Aldergate's. Not better. Just quieter." She thought of her deleted paragraphs. "I still think donations are the better model. I just can't prove we'd be the kind of newsroom that survives them."

Chaudhary capped the marker. "Vote."

They voted eleven to three to accept the money. Charlie was one of the three. Afterward, while the others gathered laptops and Lilian stacked the printed ProPublica page with the recycling, Charlie pulled the copy back out and smoothed it on the table, the crease running through the word Pulitzer.

Lilian saw her holding it. "You want to frame that or something?"

"I want to write the story about the vote," Charlie said. "Who voted, and why, and where the money came from."

"Chaudhary won't run it."

"Then I'll find out what happens when the alumni association reads it anyway." She slid the page into her binder and closed the rings. Lilian watched her do it, then pulled out her phone and started typing.

knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Concussion guidelines say an athlete with a suspected concussion should not return to play on the same day, even if they feel fine.
story:
The hit came in the sixty-second minute, a collision at the edge of the box that knocked Jazlyn flat and stopped the whistle of everything else. Alexis was twenty yards off, tracking a runner, and she heard the sound before she saw anything, a dull meeting of skull and knee that presaged the silence now spreading across the half of the field where the play had died. Jazlyn sat up almost at once. She waved off the trainer before the trainer had even reached her, and she said, twice, that she was fine, and the word fine carried so much certainty that for a second Alexis almost believed it.

Ms. Haile crouched beside her anyway. From the sideline Alexis watched the small theatre of it: the fingers Jazlyn had to follow, the questions asked too quietly to overhear, the slow shake of Jazlyn's head that was meant to end the matter. Then Jazlyn stood, dusted the turf pellets from her shorts, and turned toward the center circle, and Ms. Haile stepped in front of her, and Alexis could read the argument in their postures even at this distance, Jazlyn's chin lifted and stubborn, Ms. Haile's hands flat and immovable.

Alexis had been subbed off two minutes earlier for a cramping calf, so she was standing at the bench with a cold pack strapped to her leg when Jazlyn came storming over, stripped of her armband. "She won't let me back on," Jazlyn said, dropping onto the grass beside Alexis. "It's a playoff game. There's thirty minutes left." She pressed the heels of her hands against her eyes, then pulled them away and looked at Alexis as if Alexis had the authority to reverse it, which in a way she did, because Alexis was the captain and Ms. Haile would listen to her.

Alexis had learned the rule the hard way, in the fall of her junior year, and the memory arrived unbidden, whole. Her cousin's team at the ice rink, a November tournament, a girl on the opposing side taking a boarding hit in the second period and standing up wobbly but insistent. Alexis remembered the girl by the bench, helmet in her hands, begging to go back out before the final period, saying she felt completely normal, saying it was her last season. She remembered the rink manager, a squat man in a zippered vest, saying flatly that concussion guidelines say you don't return to play the same day with a suspected concussion, not even if you feel fine, and she remembered how the girl had cried, not from the injury but from the being kept out, and how the third period had gone on without her, skates knocking, the scoreboard indifferent.

"You can't go back on today," Alexis said now. "That's the guideline. If a concussion's suspected, you don't return the same day even if you feel fine." Jazlyn stared at her, and Alexis held the stare, though her calf ached and the game was going on without both of them now, the ball swinging across midfield where Jazlyn should have been. "You took a knee to the head," Alexis added. "They suspect it. That's the whole thing."

"I'm fine," Jazlyn said, but quieter. She looked out at the field, where her replacement, a sophomore named Casey, was playing her position with a nervous, exact diligence that would look fine to anyone who didn't know what the position was supposed to look like. Jazlyn had been recruited by two colleges already, and this game was being watched, she claimed, by an assistant coach from one of them, a claim Alexis had never fully credited but had also never challenged, because what would be the point. The scouts, the showcases, the whole extrinsic machinery of the season, mattered to Jazlyn in a way Alexis couldn't dismiss even when she wanted to, and Jazlyn's anger was not really at Ms. Haile. It was at the unfairness of a body that could betray a plan.

"I sat out a whole tournament once because of a peccadillo," Jazlyn said suddenly, a non sequitur that wasn't one. "Sophomore year. I mouthed off to a ref for one second, one stupid card, and Ms. Haile benched me for the entire weekend. I thought that was the worst thing she could do to me." She rubbed her temple without seeming to notice she was doing it, and Alexis noticed for her, and said nothing about it, and hated that she had to weigh whether saying something counted as loyalty or as betrayal.

The game tightened. With twenty minutes left the score stood at one apiece, and the wind had shifted, blowing toward Alexis's goal, and every long ball the other team launched seemed to hang against the low sun. Jazlyn coached from the grass, calling adjustments to Casey, and Ms. Haile let her, and the team absorbed the absence the way a body absorbs a missing weight, redistribution, small failures, small compensations. Alexis watched Jazlyn's hands, which never stopped moving, and her eyes, which tracked the ball with a hunger that had nothing friendly in it.

In the eighty-fourth minute, Casey scored off a corner that Jazlyn had been yelling at her to attack, and the sideline erupted, and Jazlyn was on her feet screaming with the rest of them, her head forgotten or transcended, impossible to say. When the final whistle came, one to nothing, Ms. Haile walked over and sat down in the grass between them, and for a while nobody spoke. "You did the right thing telling her," she said finally, to Alexis, and Jazlyn turned her head and looked at Alexis with an expression that Alexis would think about later, on the drive home, and again the next morning, and would never quite finish translating.

"Tomorrow," Jazlyn said, standing, pulling Alexis up by the wrist, "you're carrying my bag everywhere, and I want a smoothie, and if you tell anyone I cried at the field I will end you." She was already walking toward the parking lot, bag over her shoulder, the last light long and orange across the empty goals, and Alexis followed, her calf stiff, watching Jazlyn's steps for any wobble and not finding any, and not knowing yet whether that meant anything at all.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles.
story:
The parking lot outside the stadium smelled like charcoal and cold metal, and Carson carried the cooler while his grandfather walked ahead with the tickets held up like a passport. They had an hour before kickoff, which mattered because the stadium was running a halftime trivia contest, and Carson had signed his grandfather up for it back in September, before the season went wrong and the trips to games became apologies.

"He remembers everything," Carson had told Robin on the bus that morning, and Robin had laughed and said, "Then he'll crush it." London, headphones around her neck, had only asked what the prize was. Two seats on the fifty-yard line for next season. London had whistled at that, low, the way she did when she thought something was worth wanting.

Inside, their section was a wedge of folding seats and foil trays, and the grandfather installed himself beside a neighbor who was already unwrapping a sandwich with the ceremony of a true gourmand, commenting on the brisket he had smoked since four in the morning. The stadium noise sat over everything, quiescent in the way a held breath is quiescent, waiting for the game to give it somewhere to go.

The trivia rules were printed on a card a vendor handed out at the gate. Four questions, answered on a tablet at halftime, scored within ten minutes, and if you missed one you were out. Carson's grandfather had spent the drive reciting old facts, the kind he carried the way other people carried keys. At halftime, the screen above the field would flash the first question, and Carson knew, in the way you know a thing before you admit it, that it would be the one they had argued about in October.

In October, at the kitchen table, the grandfather had said, "I remember the very first Super Bowl like it was yesterday. Packers and the Chiefs, thirty-five to ten. I watched it on a television with one bent rabbit-ear antenna." Carson had looked at him across the plates and done the arithmetic silently. The game had been played on January 15, 1967, in Los Angeles, before either of his parents were born, and his grandfather had been born in 1963. He had not said any of this at the table. He had said, "That's amazing," and carried the dishes to the sink, and felt the shape of the lie sitting there between them, warm and unclaimed.

Now the seats filled and the teams ran their warmups, and Robin leaned over from the row behind. "Question one is history, I heard the guy at the gate say so." London had her phone out already, thumb hovering, because she believed in checking and Carson believed, or had believed, that some things shouldn't be checked in front of certain people. The grandfather was telling the brisket man about Bart Starr's receivers, the whole offense rolling down the field, and the man was transfixed, nodding along, and Carson watched his grandfather's hands moving through a game he had never seen.

The question came at halftime, silver letters on the board. Which two teams played in the first Super Bowl, on January 15, 1967, and what was the final score? The tablet screen glowed on the armrest between them, timed, ninety seconds, the countdown already bleeding.

Carson's grandfather typed the Packers. Typed the Chiefs. Typed the score, thirty-five to ten, without hesitation, and Carson sat there with London's phone dark in his pocket and the arithmetic he had done in October still true, still unspent. His grandfather could not have watched that game. He could still know it completely. Both of those things were real at once, and Carson did not know yet which one to hand the other at holidays, at funerals, at the table.

The screen ticked toward zero. The old man's finger hovered over submit, and he turned to Carson with the grin of a man holding a winning hand.

"You nervous, kid?"

Carson shook his head and watched him press the button.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed.
story:
The waiting room smelled of hand sanitizer and old carpet, and Sebastian sat with a pamphlet spread across his knee like evidence he hadn't meant to collect. Tomorrow at noon he was supposed to stand in front of thirty freshmen and explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested at a clinic like this one, a job he had volunteered for in a moment of clarity that now felt like a prank his past self had played on him. Lauren had come along partly for company and partly because she said the clinic made her nervous alone, which she admitted only after they were already on the bus.

"You could just read off the slides," she said, flipping through a magazine from 2019. "Nobody listens anyway. They're freshmen. They listen to nothing."
