"I said I'd do it properly." He turned the pamphlet over. On the back was a cartoon of a phone with a bell on it, and beneath it, in cheerful green type, SET A DAILY REMINDER. That was what had snagged him. His younger brother took no medication and couldn't keep a toothbrush routine; Sebastian had been trying to imagine explaining to a room of teenagers why a nurse would stress something as obvious as an alarm.

Across the room, a nurse was finishing with another patient, a girl maybe a year older than Sebastian, who was sliding her arms into her jacket. "So the reminder thing," the girl said, not quite looking up. "It's that important? I feel like I'd remember."

"With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy," the nurse said, handing over a small paper bag from the pharmacy window, "often because doses are missed." She said it the way she probably said it forty times a week, level and unhurried, and the girl looked at the bag in her hands for a second longer than she needed to.

Sebastian wrote it down. Not word for word, but close, because the numbers were the part he knew he would get wrong if he trusted memory. Seven out of a hundred, typical use, a year, doses missed. He could already hear how he'd want to soften it in front of the freshmen, round it down to "it's very effective," and something in him resisted that instinct. His mother did that kind of thing, smoothed edges off hard facts until they stopped meaning anything. He'd watched her do it at his grandfather's diagnosis, calling it "a rough patch," and he'd spent a long time not deciding whether it was kindness or cowardice. He still hadn't decided.

"Are you actually taking notes at the doctor?" Lauren peered over. "That's the most you thing I've ever seen."

"I'm figuring out what I'm going to say tomorrow." He hesitated, then decided to use her. "Okay. You're a freshman. I'm going to explain consent. Tell me if I sound like a motivational poster."

"Go."

He set the pamphlet aside. "It's not a form you fill out once. It's ongoing. Someone can change their mind in the middle, and stopping isn't a penalty, it's just the baseline." He kept going, kept it concrete, and when he got tangled on the difference between pressure and persuasion, Lauren said, "You just described a coercion scene from a movie," and they argued about it for five minutes until the receptionist glanced over and they lowered their voices, laughing.

"Mr. Vasquez?" The receptionist's voice broke the moment. Sebastian stood before he remembered that Vasquez was not his name, then sat back down, ears burning, while an older man rose slowly from the far corner.

When his own name came, he followed the nurse through a corridor where a poster listed what could be tested for and how, and where a second sign said, without euphemism, that results took between two days and two weeks depending on the test. He asked about the chronology of it, which tests came back when, and she answered, and he wrote that down too. There was a part of him still turbid on the whole subject, not the mechanics but the atmosphere around them, the way his own school had treated all of it as something to stigmatize rather than teach, as if naming a thing were the same as doing it. He wanted to teach it differently. He was not certain he could.

She asked if he had questions, and he did, one that wasn't on any slide. "The reminder thing. The nurse out front told that girl the pill fails more when doses get missed. If I say that tomorrow, seven in a hundred with typical use, am I going to scare them off it?"

The nurse considered him with something between amusement and respect. "That's not a medical question. That's a judgment call."

"I know," Sebastian said. He looked at his notebook, at his own handwriting already going turbid where he'd pressed too hard, and decided he would say the number straight and let it sit there unsoftened, the way the nurse had. Some of them would be scared. Some of them would set the alarm.

He walked back out through the waiting room, where Lauren was waiting with her bag already on her shoulder, and he said, "Ask me tomorrow at noon if I nailed it."

"Ask yourself," she said, and pushed the door open onto the bright afternoon street.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Silvio Berlusconi kept control of Mediaset, owner of three of Italy's main national TV channels, while serving as the country's prime minister.
story:
The coffee shop on Delancey Street had one long window that fogged whenever somebody ordered a hot drink, and by four o'clock it had gone soft with the breath of the whole afternoon. Mia had claimed the corner table because the outlet there worked, and because from there she could watch the door. Her essay on Italian media was due at midnight, and she had written ninety words of it, most of which she had already crossed out.

Rosaly came in first, shaking rain off her jacket, and Ian followed, carrying the debate like a suitcase he refused to set down. "All I'm saying," he said, dropping into the chair across from Mia, "is that if a politician owns a TV network, that's not a conflict of interest, it's just interest. Same thing."

"That's not an argument," Rosaly said. "That's a bumper sticker." She unwound her scarf and looked at Mia as if Mia might referee. Mia pulled her laptop closer, which was a way of saying she was working, and also, she realized, a way of not saying anything.

"Give me one real example," Rosaly said. "One. Somebody who actually ran a country and actually owned the networks, not in your imagination."

Ian sat back. He laced his fingers behind his head the way he did when he was about to win something. "Berlusconi," he said. "Italy. He kept control of Mediaset while he was prime minister, and Mediaset owned three of Italy's main national TV channels." He let the number sit there, three, like a card turned face up on the table.

Rosaly turned to Mia, and Mia understood she was now involved whether she had agreed to it or not. "Is that true?" Rosaly asked. "You're the one doing the paper."

Mia had a paragraph of notes open on her screen, and the fact was there, in her own handwriting from Tuesday, which made it strange to hear it spoken aloud like a weapon. "It's true," she said. "I checked." She looked at the fogged window, at the pale rectangle a bus made passing behind it. She was aware of wanting to side with Rosaly, who was her friend first, and aware also that wanting was not the same as reasoning.

"Okay," Rosaly said slowly, "so that's the example. So a prime minister with three channels. What are we supposed to do with that?"

"Admit I'm right," Ian said.

"That's not what it admits." Mia surprised herself by speaking before she had finished thinking, which her mother called her worst habit and her best one. "It admits it happened. It was legal enough to keep happening, and half the country kept voting for him anyway. So the question isn't whether it's a conflict. It's whether a rule would even fix it, or whether the rule would just ossify into something people obey on paper." She heard herself and stopped. "Sorry. I've been reading statute language all week."

Ms. Singh, who taught the media studies elective and had come in for a flat white between meetings, paused at the sugar station near their table. "That's a better sentence than most of what I graded this term," she said, and stirred her cup, and moved toward the door, and did not stay to explain anything, which was her way.

Mia turned back to the laptop. The truth was she didn't know where she stood, and the more she looked at the two of them, one certain in each direction, the more her own uncertainty seemed like a place she might actually stand in rather than a failure to arrive. Ian thought ownership was the whole story. Rosaly thought a law could fix it. Mia thought about the cashier changing the channel behind the counter, some talk show she had never watched, and about how the men on it were arguing too, and about who had chosen them.

"There's a version where he's just a businessman who never left his job," Mia said. "A sinecure he held onto while he governed. And there's a version where three channels is a seismic amount of power and nobody should have both things at once. I can't make those into one sentence yet." She typed the fact into her essay, all of it, exactly as she had written it Tuesday. Then she wrote a line under it and deleted the line and wrote it again.

Rosaly stole a sip of Mia's untouched latte. "So you're saying you don't know."

"I'm saying I know what happened," Mia said, "and I don't know yet what it means, and I have until midnight." She kept typing. Outside, the fog on the window had thinned to a clear spot the size of a hand, and through it she could see the street, and the bus stop, and the rain starting again.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In many tax systems, a deduction lowers the income that tax is calculated on, while a tax credit subtracts directly from the tax owed, so a credit is usually worth more than an equal deduction.
story:
The waiting room of Mr. Yoon's accounting office smelled of instant coffee and toner, and Riley sat beneath a framed poster of a cat dangling from a branch that said HANG IN THERE, holding his first paycheque stub like it might bite. He was sixteen, had a summer of landscaping behind him, and wanted his money back. All of it, ideally. The stub showed gross pay, then a line for income tax, then CPP and EI, then net pay, which was a smaller and more insulting number. Beside him his mother filled out a client form, and across the room a man argued with the receptionist about a receipt, waving it, truculent, insisting the sales tax was on there twice. It wasn't; Riley could see the HST line, 13 percent, added once at the bottom, exactly as the cashier at the hardware store had done every time he'd bought string trimmer line all summer.

"Riley?" Mr. Yoon appeared in the doorway, small, gray-cardiganed, holding a folder. His office held two monitors, a jar of peppermints, and a photograph of a plated croissant that suggested he was something of an epicure, or at least wished to be. "First return?"

"Yes. I worked for Meridian Landscaping, April to August." Riley set down the stub, the T4 slip that had come in the mail, and a shoebox of receipts he had kept because Dwayne had told him receipts were money. Dwayne had also told him that a guy at the gym could get him protein powder tax-free, so Riley had learned to weigh his sources.

Mr. Yoon spread the papers. "You earned income, you paid tax on it, and some of it will come back to you. Not all."

"That part I don't get. They took it. Why do I have to ask for it back?"

"That," said Mr. Yoon, "is a very good question that I am not paid enough to answer." He slid a peppermint across the desk and turned a monitor toward Riley, the return filling the screen in patient blue rows.

Riley leaned in. The cursor sat on a line near the bottom, and beside it two boxes waited to be filled. One was for tuition and education amounts. The other, further down, was something Mr. Yoon had circled in pencil, a credit for employment on a first return, small but real. Riley's first instinct was simple: bigger number first, biggest number possible. The tuition amount was much larger. He'd taken a dual-credit course at the college in the spring, and the slip said it was worth a few thousand dollars of something.

"Put the tuition in the top box," Riley said. "It's way bigger. That's the one."

Mr. Yoon said nothing, which Riley was beginning to understand was the man's entire pedagogy. He entered the tuition figure where it belonged, and Riley watched the tax owing at the bottom not change. At all. He watched Mr. Yoon type the smaller figure, the credit, into its box lower down, and the tax owing dropped, dollar for dollar, by that whole smaller amount.

"Wait." Riley put his finger on the screen. "The big one did nothing."

"The big one lowered the income the tax gets calculated on," Mr. Yoon said. "The small one comes off the tax itself."

Riley sat back. He tried to internalize it, turning it over the way he'd once turned over a carburetor in Dhruv's garage, looking for the part that made the rest move. The tuition slip, the big number, shrank the ground the tax stood on. The credit, the small number, walked up to the tax and took a bite out of it directly. So a smaller credit could be worth more than a bigger deduction, the way a twenty-dollar bill taken off your bill beat fifty dollars knocked off the price of something taxed lightly. Or however heavily. That was the part he wasn't sure of, how the rate decided which one won, and he said so.

"Now you're asking the right question," said Mr. Yoon, "and I'm still not answering it." He typed anyway, because the software answered it, and the refund at the bottom of the screen settled at a number that made Riley's mother lean forward from her chair by the window.

"That's more than I expected," she said.

"That's what the boxes are for," said Mr. Yoon.

Riley looked at the refund, then at the shoebox of receipts, still unopened on the desk. "And these? Dwayne said receipts are money."

"For a sixteen-year-old landscaper, they are mostly paper." Mr. Yoon lifted the lid, extracted the string trimmer line receipt with its tidy HST line, considered it, and set it aside. "Though if you ever buy a truck, keep everything."

The printer hummed and produced the return, still warm, smelling of the same toner as the waiting room. Riley signed where the arrows pointed, three times, his signature getting smaller each time as the boxes did. Mr. Yoon stapled the pages, filed the shoebox receipt under D for someday, and held out the peppermint jar a second time.

Riley took two.

"One for Dwayne," he said, "so he can watch me be right about something for once."

"Bring him next year," said Mr. Yoon, already opening the next folder. "I'll charge you both."

Riley pocketed the peppermints, folded his copy of the return into his back pocket, and walked out past the cat on the branch, past the man still holding his receipt at the receptionist like evidence in a trial only he was attending.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables, so customers with no orders disappear from its results entirely.
story:
Eve had the corner table by the window on the second floor of the public library, the one with the wobbly leg she steadied with her sneaker, and forty minutes before the branch closed. Mr. Kowalski had assigned it on Friday and given them the weekend, which everyone had treated as permission to forget it until Sunday afternoon. The task was simple enough to state: write a query that finds which customers in the practice database had never placed an order. Eve spread her notes across the table and opened her laptop while the rain ticked against the glass behind her.

Riley dropped into the chair opposite without asking, headphones still around her neck, laptop already open. "Tell me yours works," Riley said. "Because mine is broken, or the database is broken, or Mr. Kowalski is broken, and I need it to be one of the three before nine o'clock."

"What does it do?"

"Nothing. That's the problem." Riley turned her screen so Eve could see. The query filled most of the editor, tidy and confident, every line ending in a semicolon. Beneath it, where the results should have been, the panel said only zero rows returned. "Zero. As in, every single customer in this database has ordered something. Which is impossible, because he built inactive customers in on purpose. He told us he did."

Eve pulled her own laptop closer and typed the join the way she had planned it, matching customer IDs to order IDs, and ran it. Names scrolled past, dozens of them, every one a customer with orders. She scrolled to the bottom and counted. Then she scrolled again, slower, hunting through the list for the customers Riley insisted were there, the phantom ones, the ones who had bought nothing. The clock above the reference desk said 8:21. Downstairs, a librarian was pushing a cart through the aisles, flipping lights off row by row.

"It's not that they're missing," Eve said, mostly to herself. "It's that they can't be in the results at all." She looked at Riley's query, then at her own, and saw that they had built the same structure in different words. She highlighted the join line and stared at it the way you stare at a door you've walked through a hundred times without noticing it was a door. "We asked it to match customers to orders. So it matches them. A customer with no orders has nothing to match."

Riley leaned over the table, and for a moment they were both silent, watching the words on the screen as if the machine might betray itself further. "Then where do they go?" Riley said quietly. "They were in the table. I saw them."

"Nowhere. They just don't come out the other side." Eve thought of the customer table the way Mr. Kowalski had shown it on Thursday, forty names, and the order table with its thirty-one matches, and the gap between those numbers that she had noticed and filed away as trivia. Attrition, he had called it, half joking, the way businesses lose people without anyone deciding to lose them. She had assumed the query would surface that loss. Instead the query subjugated it, quietly, the way a form letter buries the people who never replied, and she had to admit she'd found the difference between an inner join and its alternatives only in passing, in a chapter she'd skimmed because the capricious weekend had rained and then shone and then rained again.

She deleted the line and retyped it, changing one word, then ran the query before she could second-guess it. The panel filled slowly, and then there they were: nine names, nine customers with no orders, sitting in the results as though they had been waiting the whole time. Eve sat back. Riley read the names aloud, one after another, like a roll call after a long absence. "Marisol Chen. Dmitri something with too many consonants." The library lights clicked off in the far stacks.

"Copy it," Eve said. "Change the table names so it's not identical. He'll know if we match."

"We're not cheating, we're collaborating under duress." Riley was already typing, glancing between screens. "Also I'm putting a comment in the code saying you figured it out, because if I take credit for this and then he asks me to explain it, I will subjugate myself entirely by bursting into tears." The announcement came over the speakers, ten minutes to closing, and Riley typed faster.

Eve closed her laptop halfway and watched the rain instead of the screen. It bothered her, mildly, that she still couldn't say precisely why the other join type pulled the missing rows back in, only that it did, and that tomorrow Mr. Kowalski would probably ask, and that she would have to say she knew the shape of the thing but not its whole logic. Riley snapped her laptop shut, stood, then paused with her bag half on her shoulder.

"Wait," Riley said. "Nine customers. He told us Thursday there were ten inactive ones." She looked at Eve across the table, and the last bank of lights went out behind her. "So which one of us is still missing?"

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The derivative of a function at a point equals the slope of the line tangent to its graph at that point.
story:
Jaxon would tell anyone who asked that he had calculus under control. He said it to Rayne at lunch, said it again to his father over the dishes, and now, at the kitchen table at ten at night, he said it to nobody, because the textbook had been open to the same page for forty minutes and the margin of his notebook was full of arrows that went nowhere.

The placement exam was Saturday. Mr. Clarke had mentioned it once, almost in passing, and then had spent a week being effusive about the math department at the state university, the labs, the schedule, the way first-year students who placed out of introductory calculus got first pick of electives. "Attrition in the engineering program happens in the first term," Mr. Clarke had said. "The ones who test into calc two from the start, they survive." Jaxon had heard that as a door opening. He had not heard it as a warning.

He was trying to find the maximum of a function, some polynomial the practice sheet had handed him, and the method in the book said to take the derivative and set it equal to zero. He knew the power rule, more or less. He could grind out the derivative of the polynomial, though he had gotten two different answers the two times he had done it, and he had chosen the second one because the second one came out even. That was not a reason. He knew it was not a reason, and he wrote the number down anyway.

His phone lit up. Rayne: "still studying? zachary says the tangent line thing is on the exam for sure." Jaxon typed "yeah I know that part" and put the phone face down. He did not know that part. He knew the phrase. Tangent line, derivative, slope, three words that belonged together in some way the textbook diagrams made look obvious and his own head made look like weather.

The graph paper was beside him, left over from when he used to draw floor plans for houses he invented. He plotted the polynomial by hand, point by point, plugging in values and marking them, connecting them with short careful strokes until the curve rose, flattened somewhere near the top of a hill, and came down the other side. Somewhere on that hill was the maximum. Somewhere on that hill was where his derivative was supposed to equal zero. He stared at the hill the way he had once stared at a girl across a gym, certain that staring was a form of action.

Then he remembered the ruler in his drawer, the steel one from the drafting kit, and it occurred to him that a hill has a steepest place. Near the bottom the curve climbed hard. Near the top it flattened out. If he laid the ruler against the curve so it touched at one point and matched the curve's lean at that exact point, he would have a straight line whose steepness was the curve's steepness, right there. He did it at the bottom of the hill, tilting the ruler until it kissed the curve at a single point, and counted the squares: up four, across one. At the top of the hill the ruler lay almost level, touching the peak, and the line of it was flat. Slope near zero.

"The derivative of a function at a point equals the slope of the line tangent to its graph at that point," he said out loud, in the flat voice he used for making things true by saying them. He laid the ruler at a middle point on the hill and got up two and a half over one, or close to that, the edge of the ruler not quite agreeing with itself. So the derivative at the bottom was about four, partway up it was about two and a half, and at the peak it was zero. His computed derivative, the even one he had chosen, gave a number at the bottom that was not four. He checked the other version, the first answer, the ugly one with the fraction in it, and that one gave four. He had picked the wrong answer because it was tidy.

He crossed out the tidy answer. He worked the whole thing again with the ugly one, set it equal to zero, solved, and got an x value that landed, when he plotted it, right under the flat spot at the top of the hill. He tapped the pencil against that spot twice.

The phone buzzed again. "you're fine right? you said you were fine." He looked at the ruler lying along the curve, still touching at the peak, and at the flat silver line of it against the paper. Then he picked up the phone and typed, slowly, "I was wrong, call you in ten."

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: After a LEFT JOIN, COUNT of an orders column gives 0 for customers without orders, but COUNT(*) gives 1, because it counts the NULL-filled row.
story:
The office smelled of antiseptic and old carpet, the particular combination of her mother's dental practice, and Faith had the reception computer to herself for the whole afternoon because the receptionist was at a training and her mother was in the back room doing a filling. She had promised to restock the brochure rack, an encumbrance she had put off twice already, and she had also promised herself she would finish the customer list before Kyra sent a third text asking whether it was done.

The practice had a database, cobbled together years ago by someone who had left no notes. One table held every patient who had ever been billed. A second, newer table held the orders for the whitening kits they had started selling in the spring. Kyra's job, for the business project they were doing together, had been to find out which patients had never ordered a kit, and Kyra had come back from the weekend with a report that said none. Every single patient had ordered at least once. Faith had looked at the empty shelves of the display case and thought that seemed unlikely, since about a third of the kits were still sitting there in their boxes.

She typed the query again, slowly, the way the tutorial had shown her, joining the patients to the orders with a LEFT JOIN so that every patient would stay in the result even without an order. She ran the count on the joined table using COUNT(*), and it said one for every patient, including old Mrs. Halvorsen, who had refused even to take a free sample in April because she distrusted anything with the word "cosmetic" on it. Faith leaned back in the receptionist's swivel chair and looked at the ceiling tile with the water stain shaped like a hand.

Kyra arrived at four with her laptop under her arm and her eyebrows already in a defensive position. "I ran it three times," she said, setting the laptop down beside Faith's. "Every patient has a count of at least one. I even checked Mr. Pell, and he definitely never bought anything, he thinks the kits are a scam."

"Show me your query," Faith said, and Kyra turned the screen toward her. The structure was the same as Faith's, the same LEFT JOIN, the same grouping by patient. The only difference was the count. Kyra had written COUNT(*). Faith had copied COUNT(*) from the tutorial too. She opened her own version again, put her cursor after the asterisk, and sat there.

"Do you think the join is wrong?" Kyra asked.

"Maybe it's not the join." Faith said it slowly, because she did not want to say the next part until she had tested it. She changed the asterisk to the name of the column from the orders table, the one that held the kit number, and ran it. Mrs. Halvorsen's count came back zero. Mr. Pell came back zero. A whole tail of patients Faith had never heard of, people who had moved away years ago, came back zero, and their rows in the join still existed, still showed their names, but the columns from the orders side were empty. She scrolled and scrolled and found that where there was no order, the order columns said NULL.

"The row is there," she said. "It's full of NULLs, but it's still a row."

"So the patient with no order still gets one row in the join." Kyra pulled the laptop closer and read the numbers side by side, her finger moving between the two results. "COUNT(*) gives one because it counts that NULL-filled row. COUNT of the orders column gives zero."

Faith wrote both versions out again and ran them together, watching the two numbers sit beside each other in the same result, one and zero, patient after patient. Her mother came out to say that she had cauterized a small vessel in a patient's gum and that the man was fine but complaining about the smell, and she paused behind them long enough to see two screens full of numbers. "Whatever that is," she said, "it looks like homework."

"It's the project," Kyra said. "It's due Thursday."

Faith saved both queries and named the file with the date, because she suspected she would need to show this to someone again, possibly Ellis, who had claimed the marketing section and would want to know why the customer numbers had changed overnight. Then she stood and finally restocked the brochure rack, sliding the implant pamphlets into the front slot, thinking about how the empty rows had been there all along, carrying the patients who had never ordered anything, and how a count could tell you either nothing or everything depending on which thing you asked it to count.

"Do we say the first report was wrong," Kyra asked from behind her, "or just quietly fix it?"

Faith held a pamphlet mid-air, considering whether a mistake corrected without comment counted as honest, or whether honesty meant the extra paragraph in the appendix. She slid the pamphlet into the rack.

"We'll show both numbers," she said. "And we'll say why."

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can.
story:
Kate spread the two articles across the library table like cards she had been dealt and did not want. Both concerned the same question, whether sleep deprivation measurably altered adolescent memory consolidation, and both had appeared in journals with impressive names on their spines. The first claimed a large effect. The second claimed almost none. Mr. Quinn had asked for a critical review comparing them, and Kate had assumed, when she chose the topic, that comparison meant deciding which one was right.

She read the first article again, hunting for the flaw she felt must be there. It was a single study, forty-two participants, one sleepless night each. The second was also a single study, sixty participants, three nights. She wrote "small sample" in the margin of one, then, feeling honest, wrote it in the margin of the other too. The numbers swam. Somewhere behind her, the radiator ticked like a patient clock.

Louis-Felix dropped into the chair opposite her with a granola bar and zero shame about the crumbs. "Still fighting?"

"They disagree," Kate said. "Completely. One of them has to be wrong."

"Why?" He said it the way he said most things, as though the question had genuinely never occurred to him before, which was what made him either infuriating or good company, depending on the day.

"Because they're about the same thing."

"Two people can weigh the same frog and get different numbers if their scales are bad," he said, mouth full. "That doesn't mean the frog has two weights."

Kate stared at him. Then she stared at her two articles, and a small cold thrill moved through her, the feeling of a door standing slightly open in a house she had walked past for years. If each study was a scale, and each scale was noisy, then what she wanted was not the scales but the frog. She turned to the library computer and typed her question in three different phrasings before the right result surfaced.

"Meta-analysis," she read aloud.

"What's that?"

"A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question," she said, running her finger under the sentence, "to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can." She said it again, slower, because it seemed almost too convenient, like finding out there was a machine that did exactly the thing you were failing at by hand.

Maiya arrived with tea in a thermos and a skeptical expression. "So someone just, what, pooled everyone's data? That sounds like a way to average away the interesting part. If half the studies are garbage, you've just made one big garbage smoothie."

"That's the critique," Kate said, already scrolling. "There's a whole checklist about which studies get included." She was mesmerized by the table she found: forty-one studies, sixty years of work, each a dot on a graph, and through the middle of them a line that belonged to none of them individually. The effect was real, the paper said, and smaller than her first article had claimed and larger than her second had allowed. Every single study had been partly wrong, and together they were less wrong.

She began drafting the review right there, her handwriting degrading as her thinking sharpened. The first article had sampled one night and one narrow age band, all participants from a single school, all of them similar in ways the authors never named. The second had used a broader, more phenotypically varied group and found less, which was itself a finding, or a warning, or both. She wrote a paragraph on that, then crossed out the word "clearly" four times, because nothing she was writing was clear, and the dishonesty of pretending otherwise was exactly what Mr. Quinn kept circling in red.

She found the flaw in her own argument around four o'clock, the way you find a hole in a sock. The meta-analysis could only pool the studies that had been published, and she had read, somewhere in her scrolling, that studies finding nothing often never appeared in print at all. The line through the dots might lean too high for a reason no one could see. She could not resolve it. She wrote a paragraph admitting that, and it was the hardest paragraph of the afternoon, and the one she was proudest of.

Maiya leaned over her shoulder on the way out and read the last page. "You're handing in a paper that says 'I don't know' in the final paragraph?"

"I'm handing in a paper that says I know exactly where I stop knowing," Kate said. "It's different."

Mr. Quinn was shelving returns near the door, and Kate stopped to ask whether honesty about uncertainty counted as a conclusion. He smiled and said nothing useful, which she suspected was the entire pedagogical method, and she carried her pages back to the table.

It was Louis-Felix, of all people, who found the twist, leaning over her sources an hour later with his second granola bar. "Quinn, Q.," he read off the meta-analysis's author list. "Same guy?"

Kate looked. Third author, 1998, a name that could belong to a younger Mr. Quinn with more hair and fewer red pens. She checked the acknowledgments, then the school website photo, then the gray eyes in the picture.

She picked up her pen and added a line to her review, and under it, a question.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Deliberate practice means working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, which improves skill more than simply playing through pieces already known.
story:
Rachel had learned the first movement of the Gymnopédie in a single weekend, and she had been playing it ever since, every evening, with the bedroom door shut and the window cracked so the notes could escape into the street. It was the only piece she could play all the way through. When her mother asked how the piano lessons were going, Rachel said fine, which was true in the way that most things teenagers say are true: accurate about the surface, silent about the rest.

On Thursday afternoons she took two buses to Ms. Koné's studio, a narrow room above a shoe repair shop with a metronome on the windowsill and a calendar from a year nobody had bothered to change. The calendar was anachronistic in the way the whole studio was, its appointments written in pencil and erased so many times that the paper had gone grey. Rachel sat down, opened her book to the piece she knew, and began.

Ms. Koné let her play four bars. Then she reached over, not unkindly, and lifted Rachel's hands off the keys the way you would lift a cat off a table.

"You've played this," Ms. Koné said.

"I know. I like it."

"I can hear that you like it. That's why we're going to stop." She turned to a page near the back of the book, where two bars were marked with brackets in someone else's handwriting, probably a student from years ago. "These. Just these."

Rachel looked at the bars. They required the left hand to cross over the right at speed, and the fingering felt wrong the way a word looks wrong after you stare at it. She played them. They collapsed. She played them again and they collapsed differently, which she chose to interpret as progress.

"It's called deliberate practice," said Terrance at lunch the next day. He was applying to conservatories and spoke about music with the flat certainty of someone who had already been told the rules. "You pick a specific weakness, you set a goal for it, you get feedback on it right away. It works better than playing stuff you already know. Everyone says so." He went back to his sandwich, and Rachel, who had spent the ride to school replaying the Gymnopédie in her head from memory, felt the observation land somewhere uncomfortable.

She tested it, because she was seventeen and suspicious of anything announced with that much certainty. On Saturday she played the piece she loved for an hour, start to finish, six times. On Sunday she set the metronome to half speed, put a sticky note on the two bars, and worked only on the crossing, listening after each attempt for where exactly the third finger landed late. Sunday was worse and better: worse to sit through, better to hear afterward, because at the end of the hour the crossing worked at half speed, and on Saturday it had worked at no speed at all.

The following Thursday, Ms. Koné asked for the bars first. Rachel played them, and the crossing held. Not beautifully. The dynamic was flat and her wrist was stiff, but the notes arrived in the right order at the right time, which had never once happened before.

"Now the piece," Ms. Koné said, and Rachel played the Gymnopédie, and this was the strange part: it sounded different. Not because she had improved in some general way, but because she now heard the piece as a sequence of problems, and the problems made it more interesting. The passage she used to glide over had a seam in it, and she could hear the seam.

At school, Jon had a different theory, which was that you should play whatever made you want to keep playing, because talent that quits is worth nothing. Rachel found she could not abrogate either position entirely, could not hand the whole question over to Terrance's drill or to Jon's pleasure. For a week she moved between them like a negotiator maintaining a careful detente, playing scales for an hour and then the piece she loved as a reward, telling each boy what he wanted to hear. It worked, mostly. She still did not know whether the discipline was the point or whether the discipline existed only so that the pleasure could get somewhere. Terrance would say the former. Jon would say the latter. Ms. Koné, who had a shelf of recordings she had never once explained, said nothing on the subject at all.

What Rachel decided, in the end, was smaller than a decision: the two bars were the assignment, and the piece was the reason, and if one of them ever stopped leading back to the other she would notice. She wrote the two bars on an index card and kept it in the front pocket of her backpack, where the corners would go soft over the winter.

In April there was a small recital in the studio above the shoe repair shop, six students on folding chairs, parents standing at the back near the door. Rachel played the Gymnopédie, all of it, and when she reached the crossing her hands moved without her asking them to, and the seam she had learned to hear closed quietly under her fingers. Afterward Ms. Koné was talking to a parent near the metronome, so Rachel packed her own book into her bag. The index card was still in the front pocket, softened at the corners. She took it out, looked at the two bars, and slid it back in.

"Same time next week," Ms. Koné called from across the room, already turning back to the parent. "Bring the book. We start the next one."

Rachel zipped the bag and said, "I already looked at it. The first page has this arpeggio."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched.
story:
Charles had planned to spend the last Friday of summer in the pool at Ria's building, but his mother's office was short-staffed and the apartment was being fumigated, so he sat in a swivel chair by the window with a badge that read VISITOR and his phone hot in his hand. The video had reached him an hour earlier: a flooded street, brown water to the door handles, a man in a kayak paddling past a pharmacy. The caption said it was downtown that morning, and Abbie had already sent it to the group chat with three exclamation marks and the question, should we warn everyone?

He wanted to share it. That was the honest part of the impulse; he wanted to be the one who had told people first, and a quieter part of him suspected that wanting was exactly the problem. His mother had once said that a rumor spreads the way an alluvial fan spreads, depositing everything it carries in the widest possible shape, and he had rolled his eyes at the time, but the metaphor had stuck like a burr.

At the desk across from his mother's, a man named Mr. Wiśniewski was eating soup with great concentration. Charles had met him twice before and liked him because he told jokes with the timing of someone who had rehearsed them alone. When Charles sighed loudly for the third time, Mr. Wiśniewski set down his spoon.

"You look like a man watching his team lose," he said.

"Trying to figure out if a video is real," Charles said. "Or new, anyway. It says this morning but the light looks weird." He came over and held out the phone, and Mr. Wiśniewski tilted his glasses down to look, which Charles found both comic and somehow reassuring, like a jeweler appraising a suspicious stone.

"There's a plugin for this," Mr. Wiśniewski said, and pulled Charles around to his own monitor. "InVID-WeVerify," he said, pronouncing it carefully. "A European Union-funded project built it." He dropped the video's link into a panel, and the plugin split the video into key frames, a strip of stills laid out like film negatives on a lightbox. "Now you can search the frames," he said, and that was all he said, folding his arms and leaving the rest to Charles, which Charles understood as deliberate and was grateful for.

He dragged the clearest frame, the one with the pharmacy sign, into a reverse image search. Nothing. He tried the second frame, the one with the kayak, and there it was, on a local news site dated almost two years ago, a different city entirely, a different flood. He sat back. The video was real in one sense, water and all, and a lie in the sense that mattered, and both things were true at once, which was not a paradox so much as a plain fact he had never had to hold before. He was honest enough with himself to admit he still couldn't prove the caption was a lie rather than a mistake, and that the difference between those two was itself something he couldn't verify from here.

He texted Abbie instead of the group chat, then thought better of it and posted both links side by side, the video and the news article, with one line: "found the original, it's from two years ago." Ria replied with a single relief-faced emoji and "good catch," and someone he didn't know replied "how did you do that," and he started typing an answer and stopped, because the honest answer was that a man with soup had pointed at a door and Charles had walked through it.

When he turned around, Mr. Wiśniewski was holding out a cup of coffee, the bad office kind, cream and two sugars already in it. "For the detective," he said. Charles took it. He was about to make a joke about the kayak man, about how a single flood had become a synecdoche for every flood, a part standing in for a whole weather system of anxiety, but then he closed his mouth, because Mr. Wiśniewski would ask him to define the word, and Charles would prevaricate, claiming he'd learned it in English class, when really he'd learned it from his mother, along with the thing about rivers.

Instead he said, "Can I see how you did the key frames again? Next time I want to do it myself."

Mr. Wiśniewski dragged the soup bowl aside and patted the chair beside him.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under the legal rule called contra proferentem, used in many jurisdictions, an ambiguous term in a contract is usually read against the party that wrote it.
story:
The envelope had been on the kitchen table for nine days before Isabelle opened it, which her mother said was an indictment of her entire approach to adult life, though her mother said it while refilling the kettle, so it did not land as severely as intended. Inside was a bill for four hundred and twelve dollars from the phone company, itemized under a line that read, simply, "unlimited plus overage." Isabelle read it four times. She had signed up for the unlimited plan in August, alone, at the mall, because she was seventeen and about to start college and wanted to feel like someone who handled things. The clerk had slid a tablet across the counter and asked for her signature, and she had given it, printed and cursive, the way the form demanded, without reading anything except the price at the top.

She spread the contract on the table now, beside the cereal bowl and her half-finished application for on-campus housing. The words were small and recalcitrant, refusing to resolve into sense no matter how she squinted. Unlimited plus overage. Her thumb found the phrase and stayed there. Either unlimited meant unlimited, or it did not, and if it did not, then what was the plus doing? She could hear her father in the other room describing the situation to his brother, saying the words "predatory" and "boilerplate" with the satisfaction of a man who had recently learned them.

Coleton came over after his shift, still smelling faintly of the coffee shop, and sat down across from her. He read the bill upside down first, then right side up, which was his habit. "You used how much data?"

"Forty gigabytes. Moving my grandmother's photos. I asked the guy if unlimited covered it and he said, and I quote, basically."

"Basically is not a legal term."

"Neither is unlimited plus overage," Isabelle said, "and yet."

They called the company together, on speaker, and the hold music was a version of something that had once been a song. The representative, when she arrived, was courteous in the way of someone reading from a screen. The overage, she explained, was applied per the terms and conditions, which Isabelle had agreed to by signature. Isabelle said the line was ambiguous. The representative said the line was clear. Isabelle said that a thing could not be both unlimited and overaged at once, and the representative said that she understood the frustration, which was a different thing entirely.

It was Coleton, later, who found it, though Isabelle was the one who recognized what it was. He had gone looking through a consumer law site for something, anything, and started reading aloud from his phone at the table, his mouth full of the toast her mother had made him without being asked. "Here. Under the legal rule called contra proferentem, an ambiguous term in a contract is usually read against the party that wrote it."

Isabelle put down her fork. "Say that again."

He said it again, slower, crumbs and all. She copied the phrase onto the back of the housing application and looked at it. The party that wrote it. Not the party that signed it, not the seventeen-year-old at the mall with her thumb hovering over a screen. The company had drafted the line; the company got to live with what the line failed to say. It did not erase her signature. It did not refund her naivety. It meant, if she understood it, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she only half did, that the fog belonged to whoever had made it.

From the doorway, her mother watched the two of them bent over the table, the contract flattened under Isabelle's elbow, Coleton's phone passed back and forth like something warm. She had spent the afternoon titrating her own involvement, adding a little advice here, withholding a little there, wanting her daughter to fight this one alone but not quite alone. She had signed contracts of her own in her life, some of them without reading, and she did not say this.

Isabelle wrote a letter at the table that night, longhand first, then typed. She quoted the line, quoted the rule, cited nothing she could not point to on paper. She ended it with a request that the charge be removed, and she printed two copies, and signed only one of them, the way she had learned you did with things that mattered.

"Sealed envelope, mailbox, tomorrow," Coleton said, sliding the second copy into his backpack for safekeeping.

Isabelle ran her thumb once more along the phrase she had copied, the foreign words sitting there in her own handwriting, and then licked the envelope shut.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A plagal cadence moves from the IV chord to the I chord and is often called the 'Amen cadence' because many hymns sing 'Amen' to it.
story:
The practice room smelled like dust and old radiators, and Hannah had claimed it for the last hour before the building emptied. Her assignment sat on the music stand in her own handwriting, sixteen bars of a melody for Mr. Rowe's theory class, and fifteen of them were finished. The sixteenth bar was a blank staff with a pencil mark hovering above it, drawn back so many times it had worn a small grey cloud into the paper.

The problem was the ending. Her melody had started in the practice room on Tuesday, a phrase she had caught herself humming while walking home, and it had grown bar by bar all week. But now it arrived at the final measure and stopped, like a sentence that had lost its nerve. She had tried ending on the tonic chord, the obvious homecoming, and it had sounded like a door slamming. She had tried holding the note longer, which had only made the door slamming slower.

She played it through again, right hand only, then added the left hand chords she had sketched in. The chord changes were supposed to be her own, Mr. Rowe had said, not borrowed from a song, and she had labored over each one until the harmony felt like something she had actually chosen. But the last change defeated her. Every option she played either debilitated the melody, dragging it into something heavy, or threw it away, ending so lightly it seemed to have wandered off rather than concluded.

The door opened without a knock. Joseph stood in the frame with his trumpet case, already apologizing. "Rowe said this room was free. There's a wait for the other ones."

"It's fine. I'm nearly done." She was not nearly done, and he could probably see that from her face.

He set the case down but didn't open it. Instead he leaned against the wall and listened while she played the fifteen bars again, out of stubbornness, so he would understand the size of the problem. When she stopped before the last measure, he said, "It wants to land softer. Mine kept doing that."

"Yours is done?"

"For a week now. It's not great, but it's done." He came over and looked at her page, tilting his head. "You wrote all the chords already?"

"Except the last one. That's the whole disaster."

He hummed his own ending then, not on the trumpet, just his voice, quiet and a little self-conscious in the small room. She heard his melody climb, settle, and then, at the very end, two chords in succession that made her sit up straight on the bench. The first was the chord built on the fourth degree of his key. The second was the tonic. IV to I, and something in the sound was instantly familiar, like recognizing a face across a street before you can place the name.

"That," she said. "What is that?"

"That's my ending. My grandma hums it. She sings in church, and at the end of every hymn she does those two chords while everyone says the last word. I stole it from her basically." He hummed it again, slower, and this time he sang the word along with it: "Amen." The two chords fell the way the word falls, final but gentle, an agreement rather than a slam.

"The plagal cadence," Hannah said, mostly to herself, and Joseph shrugged, because he hadn't called it anything. She pulled her theory notebook out of her bag and flipped to the page from last week's class. There it was in her notes: IV to I. The plagal cadence. She had written it down without hearing it, a label on an empty box, and now Joseph's grandmother had filled the box with sound. She remembered Mr. Rowe mentioning that hymns sang "Amen" over it, and she hadn't understood then what he meant, that the word and the chords had grown around each other until neither could be heard alone.

"It's called the Amen cadence," Joseph said, reading over her shoulder. "It's in the book too, I think. Emerik told me. He's been calling every ending that all week."

She played it in her own key. The fourth degree's chord first, then home, with the final melody note held over both. It was like the difference between being told to go to your room and being allowed to finish the evening first. The melody that had been straining toward an ending now simply settled into one, and the sixteenth bar filled itself in under her pencil: the bass moving down a step, the melody resting on the tonic, the whole thing sounding as though it had always known where it was going.

Then she stopped, because it was almost too easy, and she didn't trust easy. She played the ending three more times, and each time she liked it and doubted it in equal measure. It was a borrowed sound, a hundred years of Sunday mornings borrowed through Joseph's grandmother, and part of her wondered whether her melody had actually earned it, or whether she had just found a door that happened to fit her key. She thought of the way the piece was built, its phrases small and interchangeable, and she liked that modularity, the way the opening phrase could return in bar nine without seeming out of place. A piece that rearranged itself that freely might deserve an ending that didn't insist on its own importance. Or it might not. She could hear both arguments and could not choose between them, and Mr. Rowe had never once promised that theory would choose for you.

"Play the whole thing," Joseph said, so she did, all sixteen bars, both hands, and when the last two chords came he smiled a little, the way people do at a familiar word in an unfamiliar sentence.

The radiator ticked. Outside the window the afternoon was already thinning, the school settling into its diurnal emptying, hallway lights going off in sections while the custodian worked his way down the corridor. Hannah sat with her hands still on the keys, looking at the completed page, the pencil cloud finally replaced by notes.

"Your grandma has good taste," she said.

"She'll be glad somebody thinks so," Joseph said, picking up his trumpet case. "Play it again before you pack up. I want to hear the Amen part once more."

She set her fingers on the keys.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: The doctrine of double effect, traced to Thomas Aquinas, holds that causing a harm one foresees but does not intend can be permissible when it is a side effect of pursuing a good end.
story:
The volunteer badge itched against Jackson's chest, and he scratched at it while the charge nurse explained the morning: refill water pitchers on Four West, don't linger, don't answer questions about anything medical. He needed the hours. Sixty of them, documented, or the health careers scholarship would go to someone else, and his mother had already told the relatives he was getting it. That was the part that sat wrong, he thought as he pushed the squeaking cart down the corridor. He had not exactly said he would win. He had only let everyone believe it.

On Four West the rooms were quiet in the way of people waiting for something to be decided. In 412 a family had gathered around a bed where an old woman slept with her mouth open, thin as paper. Jackson stood in the doorway with his pitcher and heard a young man's voice, tight and furious. "You're telling me the pain medicine could kill her. You're saying that out loud like it's normal."

"I'm saying it could shorten her life," the doctor said. "It's not what we intend. We intend to keep her comfortable. That distinction matters. It's called the doctrine of double effect, and it goes back to Thomas Aquinas. A harm you foresee but don't intend can be permissible when it's a side effect of a good end."

The young man laughed, ugly and short. "Philosophy. My grandmother is not a thought experiment." He was maybe twenty-five, chinos and a lanyard from some office, and he kept saying the word deposition the way other people said a door slamming. If the hospital moved forward without consent, his lawyer would take depositions from everyone involved, and he would lambaste them publicly, he said, in the paper if he had to. The doctor's shoulders lowered half an inch, which Jackson noticed, because the doctor's shoulders were the only calm thing in the room.

Jackson should have backed away. Instead he filled the pitcher at the sink, and the young man turned on him. "You. You're here all the time, right? You see what they actually do." Jackson said he just brought water. The young man came closer. "Have you seen her awake? Awake and asking for anything?" And Jackson, wanting to be useful, wanting to matter even a little, said, "She was awake Tuesday. She seemed pretty out of it." That was true. She had seemed out of it. But he had not seen her ask for anything, or refuse anything, and he let the young man assume he had.

The assumption traveled fast. By lunch the family had filed a complaint, and the charge nurse found Jackson in the supply room and asked what he had told them. His answer took four seconds, and he watched his scholarship shrink in her face. Not withdrawn, she said carefully, but documented, and documentation follows you. Responsibility, she said, was not the same as blame, though she did not explain the difference, and Jackson carried both out of the room with him.

He went back to 412 after his shift. The young man was alone now, sitting in the visitor's chair with his phone dark in his hand, and Jackson told him the whole truth: Tuesday he had refilled water, the old woman had seemed groggy, and everything beyond that had come from the grandson's own mouth, not Jackson's. He apologized without softening it. The young man stared at the floor a long moment, then at the bed. "She told me once she didn't want to be kept here like a project," he said. "Last year, when she was herself. I keep trying to remember if she meant it." He said the family had spent the morning arguing about what she would want versus what they could live with, and nobody could win both. Jackson said the doctor's line back to him, about the harm you foresee but don't intend. "Yeah," the young man said. "Except she's the consequence either way."

The woman in the bed shifted and opened her eyes, and Jackson, standing closest, hesitated with one hand on the rail. He still didn't know whether the family would sign the consent form, whether his incident report would sink the scholarship, or whether he had made anything better by coming clean or only smaller and cleaner, like a room swept after the flood. On his way out he passed the nurse's station and saw the doctor signing something at the counter, the same half-lowered shoulders, going on to the next door. The young man came into the hallway behind him and called out, "Hey. Water boy." Jackson turned. "If she pulls through," the young man said, "I'll bring her a card. If she doesn't, I'll know it wasn't you."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: The United Kingdom's standard rate of VAT, a sales tax built into most prices, has been 20 percent since January 4, 2011.
story:
Jasmine counted the bills twice before the register drawer swallowed them. Six weeks into the job at Mr. Islam's hardware store, she had finally acclimated to the smell of linseed oil and the clatter the till made at closing, though she still flinched when the bell over the door rang after nine. Her first real paycheque lay folded in her back pocket, and it was wrong, or it felt wrong: she had multiplied her hours by her wage and arrived at a number $80 higher than the deposit that had landed in her account. CPP, EI, income tax, the stub said, in columns she read under the counter lamp like a foreign language.

The camera was the problem. A used Canon film body sat in a display case at the pawnshop three blocks east, priced at $310, and Ashlyn had texted that morning to say the owner was "making noises about selling it to some guy from out of town." Jasmine texted back that she'd have the money by Friday. Then she did the arithmetic again on a scrap of receipt paper, adding the sales tax she'd forgotten to include, and watched her plan come up $41 short.

Timothe found her on her break, hunched over her phone outside the store with the pawnshop's listing open. He was holding his own phone sideways, comparing a UK auction site. "Look at this," he said, tilting the screen toward her. "Same body, same lens, and the price is way lower."

Jasmine looked. Lower, yes, but something snagged in her mind, and she scrolled to the site's fine print instead of trusting the sticker. "It's called VAT," she read aloud. "Value added tax. In the UK it's built into the sticker, twenty percent, and it's been twenty percent since January the fourth, 2011." The words sat there plainly, a fact she hadn't known an hour ago and now couldn't unknow.

"Which means what for us?" Timothe asked.

She pulled out the receipt paper and worked it through, slowly, because she'd been burned once already tonight. The UK price had the tax already folded inside it, invisible, finished. The Canadian price at the pawnshop wore its tax on the outside; thirteen percent got bolted on at the till. She wrote both final numbers down, circled them, and felt something tectonic shift in her scheme. The cheap UK camera wasn't cheap. Between shipping and currency, the arbitrage she'd been dreaming about for ten minutes simply dissolved. The local camera, tax and all, was still the better number, and it was still $41 beyond her.

"I can cover you," Timothe offered.

"You're saving for residence. No."

She went back inside and did the closing count, and it was there, slowed to a crawl, that she noticed what she'd been too busy to see all week: the shelf of brass fittings half empty with no reorder tag, the "BACK IN 5" sign Mr. Islam had taped up on Tuesday and never taken down, the landlord's envelope on the desk with its window showing a sum far larger than anything a hardware store on this street should owe. Her stomach tightened. She counted the drawer a third time, unnecessarily, because her hands needed something to do.

The bell rang at 9:40. Mr. Islam came in with wet shoes and a folded letter, and he set it on the counter between them while he counted the floats for tomorrow, which she understood, in the moment before he spoke, was a tomorrow that probably didn't include her.

"Read it later, at home," he said. "It's for you. And there's an envelope in the drawer with your name."

She waited until she was on the bus, wedged against the window with the letter open on her knee. His handwriting slanted uphill. The lease was ending, he wrote, and the new one wasn't survivable, so the shop would close at the end of the month, and he was sorry, sorrier than the letter could hold. He had done her final pay himself, by hand, and he suspected he had over-deducted her in the first month; the extra envelope was the difference, plus a little for the camera he'd heard her talk about with the boy who smelled of bus shelter. She opened the envelope under the streetlights at her stop. Inside, alongside the bills, was a strip of brass fitting, the small kind, wrapped in a receipt from the very first day she'd worked there.

On Friday she walked to the pawnshop with the full amount, tax included, counted out at the till. Ashlyn was already there, nose against the glass. "You got it," Ashlyn said.

"He got it," Jasmine said, and tapped the case. "The guy from out of town."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The 1947 Taft-Hartley Act, passed over President Truman's veto, allowed US states to pass right-to-work laws banning contracts that require workers to pay union fees.
story:
Charles set the extra plates before his father got home, wiping each one twice because the dishwasher left a film. Anika and Ella were coming straight from the warehouse, and his mother had put a pot of chili on the stove big enough for six, though it would be four of them plus his father, whose shift at the plant ended at seven.

The two of them arrived together, still in their work vests, and sat down in the chairs Charles had wiped. Anika had transferred from the distribution center in her old state two months ago; Ella had come the other direction, from a state whose name she kept saying like a credential. They had been arguing since the parking lot, and they brought the argument to the table like a dish neither would put down.

"He says I have to sign the dues checkoff by Friday or I'm off the schedule," Anika said, tearing a piece of bread in half without eating it. "Where I'm from, nobody made me pay anything. I never signed a thing."

"Because your state had a right-to-work law," Ella said. "This one doesn't. Here the contract requires it, everybody pays, that's the whole point. If some people don't pay, they still get the raise the rest of us fought for."

Charles ladled chili while they went back and forth. He had his own Friday deadline: the same checkoff card sat folded in his locker, unsigned, and the twenty-six dollars a pay period mattered concretely against the tuition deposit due in August. He had been letting the card sit there the way his father let bills sit face down on the counter.

His father came in still smelling of coolant, washed his hands at the kitchen sink, and sat down. When Anika explained the dispute, he set his spoon down and said only that in his local, everyone paid, and that a man who took the wage without the dues was letting everyone else carry him. It wasn't a speech; it was four sentences, and then he asked for the cornbread.

Ella turned to Charles. "You haven't signed either. What are you doing?"

"Holding off." He said it evenly, though he had not admitted this to anyone. "I wanted to know what the law actually is first. Not what the steward says, not what the flyer says."

He took out his phone under the table, then brought it up openly and typed. It took him three searches to get past opinion pieces, and then he found the statute summary and read it slowly enough to catch the shape of it. The Taft-Hartley Act, 1947, passed over President Truman's veto. It allowed states to pass right-to-work laws, banning contracts that required workers to pay union fees. He read the line twice, then set the phone flat on the table between the chili and the bread basket, screen up, so they could all see it.

"So both of you are right," he said. "The state Anika came from passed one of those laws after Taft-Hartley made it possible. Ella's didn't. Same company, same union, different states, different rules." He paused, because the next part was the part he had been circling all week. "But the law being on your side isn't the same as the question being settled. The union here negotiated the wage scale. The eleven-fifty Anika makes now instead of minimum is because somebody paid dues before she got hired."

"Freedom of choice," Anika said, but quieter than she'd said anything all evening.

His father reached past the phone for the cornbread. "In my grandfather's day they'd have called a man who thought like that judicious," he said. "It meant he weighed things. Half the time it just meant he was slow to commit."

They kept eating. Charles turned the fact over alongside the older one, the one from his history class, that collective bargaining had not existed in any formal sense since antiquity, that it was a modern invention people had been jailed for, and that the laws permitting it were newer than his grandmother. Two of his coworkers had moved from two different states and arrived at the same warehouse with two different ideas of what was owed. His father thought the answer was obvious. Anika thought the opposite was obvious. Charles found he could hold both positions at once without pretending they fit together, and what stayed uncertain was the only thing that was actually his to decide.

"What about the vote?" Ella said suddenly, straightening. "The contract ratification. It's next month. If you're in the bargaining unit, you vote whether you pay or not. Sign the card, vote however you want, that's the system."

Anika looked at the phone still glowing on the tablecloth, then at Charles. "Would you split the fee with me?" she asked. "Half each, if it's really about the money."

Charles picked up his spoon and finished the chili in his bowl before he answered. "Bring your card Friday," he said. "We'll sign them at the same table."

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The Soviet Union diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton, and the shrinking, saltier Aral Sea lost a fishing industry that had employed about 40,000 people.
story:
The tomatoes went limp in the third week of June, and nobody at the Delancey community garden could say why. Jonathan knelt in the mulch beside row four and pressed a finger into the drip line, which should have been sweating water into the soil since dawn and was bone dry. Madalyn crouched next to him and followed the black tubing back toward the spigot on the shed, calling out that the pressure was fine on her side, that her peppers had drunk their fill the day before. Simona stood at the fence with the water bill in her hand, the one Ms. Guo had asked her to fetch, and read the number out loud twice because nobody believed it the first time.

They had turned the water on in April, all of them together, and Jonathan remembered that morning the way you remember weather. Ms. Guo had let the spigot hiss and then settle into its steady trickle while Madalyn named every seedling like a christening and Simona argued for a row of something they could actually sell at the Saturday table. Jonathan had carried the tomato flats two at a time, careful of the stems, and his father had driven past on his way to the site and honked. That was before the bill, before the crinkle of brown creeping up the lower leaves like a tide going out.

Ms. Guo did not explain anything, which was her way. She asked who was upstream of them, and when nobody answered, she asked it again, slower, and then went to argue with the landlord's office downtown. That left the three of them with the dry rows and Simona's phone and a long afternoon. Jonathan typed water diverted upstream who loses and read while the sun moved across the plot, and what he found stopped him so completely that he read it aloud.

The Soviet Union, he read, had diverted the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton. Whole cotton fields where there had been nothing drinkable. And the Aral Sea, which those rivers fed, had shrunk and grown saltier until the fishing industry that had employed about forty thousand people was gone. He said the number again. Forty thousand. Madalyn took the phone from him and read it herself, as if his voice might have rounded it wrong.

It enthralled him in a way he was slightly ashamed of, the way disasters can, because it was so clean and so large. A country wants cotton, so it turns two rivers aside, and at the far end of the water a sea starts to die and forty thousand fishermen pack up their nets. Simona, still scrolling, said it was like dominoes except you couldn't see the dominoes, only the last one falling. Madalyn said it was more like a heurraistic, and then corrected herself, a heuristic, something you could use to look at anything: follow the water, and whoever is standing at the bottom of the hill is the one who gets hurt. Jonathan thought about their spigot, and about who might be standing at the top of their particular hill.

The landlord's office gave Ms. Guo a shrug and a printout. The city had resold a portion of the water allocation for the block, effective the first of June, to the developer putting up the Meridian complex on Delancey and Fourth. The plot's allocation had been cut to a fraction, which explained the bill, which explained the tomatoes. Simona said the name of the developer out loud before she thought, and then stopped, and looked at Jonathan, because he had already gone pale and there was no way to unring it.

His father was the site supervisor at Meridian. He had been out of work for eight months before that job, and the spring Jonathan remembered, the honk from the truck, had been the sound of a man with a paycheck. Jonathan had known the complex was going up, had even driven past the crane with him, but he had never once followed the water. Now the connection was undeniable and seismic in the small scale of his life: the concrete being poured at Fourth Street was drinking from the same cup as row four.

He didn't say anything for the rest of the afternoon. He hauled the two rain barrels from behind the shed, the ones they'd never gotten around to hooking up, and Madalyn found a tarp and rigged a catchment off the shed roof, and Simona called a guy at the extension office about gray water, whoever he was, and left a message that was mostly apologizing. They would save some of the garden and lose some of it, and everyone understood that without saying it. Ms. Guo came back near closing and looked at the tarp, the barrels, the buckets standing in a line like a bucket brigade for a fire not yet out.

At home, Jonathan asked his father over dinner how much water the Meridian site was using. His father said enough, why, and Jonathan said no reason, and both of them let it sit there between the plates. He thought about telling the others to take the story of his father's job out of the group chat, or about telling his father about the forty thousand fishermen, and did neither, because he wasn't sure which request he could live with making, or which answer.

On Saturday they sold what had survived, three baskets of peppers and a sad heap of squash, and Madalyn taped a sign to the table that read Save Delancey Garden, Water Is Not Guaranteed, and people stopped who would not have stopped for vegetables alone. An older woman in a sun hat put two dollars in the jar without taking anything, and stood a while reading the sign, and asked Madalyn what river it was again that they'd turned aside. "The Amu Darya," Madalyn said. "And the Syr Darya. And the sea was the Aral."

Jonathan was stacking the empty baskets when his phone buzzed: his father, from the site, a photo of the crane against the morning sky with no caption at all. He looked at it for a long moment, then put the phone face down on the table and went to help Simona carry the barrels back to the shed.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Antoine arrived at the Rialto twenty minutes early, which he immediately regretted, because it gave him time to stand under the marquee rehearsing everything that could go wrong. Thea showed up seven minutes later in a green coat, carrying the two tickets she had insisted on buying, since she was the one who had chosen the film. "You're punctual," she said, and he could not tell whether that was a compliment or an accusation.

At the concession stand he ordered a large popcorn, and the cashier, without asking, added a free upgrade because the medium machine was broken. The bucket was absurd, munificent beyond anything two people could reasonably eat, and Thea laughed at the size of it, which felt like a point in his favor. She took the first handful before the lights dimmed, which meant she would have to reach past him or ask for the rest of the evening, and Antoine noticed that she angled the bucket toward her own knee instead, keeping it accessible to both of them. He thought about doing something similar with his arm on the armrest and then thought better of it.

The film itself was built to beguile, all long shots and a score that swelled at exactly the right moments, and for most of it Antoine forgot to be nervous. Then, forty minutes in, he reached for popcorn at the same moment she did, and their hands collided, and he withdrew so fast that he knocked the bucket against his own chest. A few kernels scattered into the aisle. She whispered, "It's fine," but he spent the next half hour cataloguing the incident alongside everything else: the joke he had made before the previews that had landed flat, the moment he had asked if she wanted the armrest and she had said, "Either way," which was the least committal sentence in the English language.

Afterward, in the lobby, she said she had to check the bus schedule, which he interpreted as a coded exit. They stood by the doors while she scrolled her phone. He offered her the rest of the popcorn, tipped toward her like evidence, and she took a single piece and said, "It's a forty-minute wait."

"You can call your mom," he said. "I can wait with you, or."

"Or," she said, smiling at the word. "Or is an option."
