Outside, the night had gone cold, and she was in the green coat and he was not in much of anything, so he did not offer a jacket he did not have and instead walked them to the shelter and stood on the windward side of her, which she noticed, because she said, "That's very chivalrous of the popcorn bucket," and moved it so that it blocked the wind instead of him.

His mind, meanwhile, had begun its own quiet casuistry, laying out arguments for why the evening had been a disaster: the flat joke, the hand collision, the forty-minute wait she was clearly enduring rather than enjoying. He was well into the case against himself when he remembered Jacqueline, weeks ago, in the library, leaning over a printed article she was supposed to be summarizing for psychology. "Erica Boothby," she had said. "2018. After a first conversation, people underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. They call it the liking gap." He had barely listened at the time; it had sounded like one more thing adults said to make teenagers feel better. But he listened now, watching Thea's face in the light of the bus schedule.

He tested it the only way he could, which was to ask directly, and asking directly felt like stepping off something. "Can I say something weird," he said. "I keep thinking tonight went badly. From my side, I mean. That you were bored."

Thea looked up from her phone. "You thought I was bored. I thought you were bored. I picked a slow movie and you didn't complain once, so I assumed you were being polite." She turned the phone face-down on her knee. "I looked up showtimes for this three weeks ago. Before I even asked you."

The bus came early, brakes gasping under the streetlight, and she stood and handed him the popcorn bucket, which was still a third full. "You carry it," she said. "You're better at sharing than you think." She stepped up onto the bus, tapped her card, and then turned around in the doorway, holding it open while the driver waited. "Saturday?" she said. "There's a matinee. I'll buy the tickets again, and you can pick something terrible this time."

"Something terrible," Antoine agreed, and the doors closed on her smile, and he stood holding the warm bucket of popcorn in the cold, watching the taillights diminish down the avenue.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: The US Plain Writing Act, signed by President Barack Obama on October 13, 2010, requires federal agencies to write documents for the public in clear, plain language.
story:
The form was four pages long, and Aaron had read the third paragraph six times without it yielding anything like a meaning. He sat at the kitchen table with a pen cap between his teeth, the afternoon light going copper on the paper. Section 2 asked him to attest that the statements in Section 1 were accurate "to the best of his knowledge and belief, in consonance with applicable provisions." He understood each word separately. Together they might as well have been a locked door.

"Did you finish it?" his mother asked from the stove.

"I don't even know what it wants from me."

He needed the job. The bookstore two bus transfers away was hiring for the summer, and the interview was Thursday, and the paperwork had to come with him. On Tuesday he texted Luka, who had a job at the pool and had survived the same form. Luka sent back a photo of his own completed pages, half the boxes marked in what looked like guesswork, and the message "i just picked the one that sounded least wrong." That was one way through. Aaron wanted a better one, though he couldn't have said why the difference mattered so much, only that filling a form by guessing felt like a small surrender.

At school he asked Yasmin, who was applying for a congressional internship and therefore fluent in bureaucracy. She pulled up the agency's website on her phone outside the cafeteria. "Look," she said, scrolling. "There's a whole plain language section. They're supposed to write these things clearly. It's a law." She read for a moment, lips moving. "The Plain Writing Act. Signed by Obama on October thirteenth, twenty ten. Federal agencies have to write documents for the public in clear, plain language."

"Then why is mine like this?"

"Maybe it's old. Or maybe nobody made them fix it." She shrugged and handed the phone over so he could see the page himself. He read it twice, and something in him sat up straighter. There was a standard, and the form fell short of it, and the failing was not his.

Wednesday night he wrote an email to the agency's help address. His first draft began "I am writing to express my profound frustration," and he deleted it, because complaining in a way designed to aggrandize his own annoyance would get him nothing. He rewrote it plainly. He stated which form, which section, what he could not understand, and what he needed to know to complete it. He asked his question in a numbered list. He signed it with his full name and phone number, and then, after a minute's thought, he cut the sentence where he'd called the form "obsolescent," because he wasn't certain that was the right word for a form that had never worked, and he didn't want to sound like a kid reaching for vocabulary he couldn't hold.

On Thursday, in a shirt with a collar that felt like a costume, he sat across from Ms. Gupta in the bookstore's back office, the interview going well until it wasn't going anywhere at all. She asked the usual questions and he answered them, and then she slid a sample of their staff handbook across the desk. "We're revising this. Tell me what you notice."

He read a paragraph about scheduling that contradicted itself twice, and another that used the word "utilize" four times. "It's hard to follow," he said.

"Good. How would you fix it?"

"Shorter sentences. Say 'use.' And when two rules conflict, pick one and say which one wins." He hesitated, then decided to say it anyway. "I spent this week fighting a federal form that was worse than this. There's a law, the Plain Writing Act, signed in twenty ten by Obama, that makes federal agencies write clearly for the public. Your handbook isn't federal, so the law doesn't touch it. But it's a decent standard anyway."

Ms. Gupta leaned back. "The law doesn't touch us, so why should we care?"

"Because I lost two evenings to that form, and I almost guessed my way through it, and guessing on paperwork that matters is how people get hurt." He kept his voice level, though his pulse was up. "You can disagree. Plenty of people think plain style dumbs things down."

"I don't think that," she said. "I think it's harder to write short than long. Most people can't do it."

"I can," Aaron said, and then, because honesty was the whole point, "or I'm learning to."

She wrote something on her pad. "Bring the email you sent the agency. The one with the numbered list. I want to see it."

"It's on my phone." He was already reaching for his pocket.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Ray Oldenburg's 1989 book The Great Good Place named 'third places', such as cafes and libraries, where people meet outside home and work.
story:
The first thing Aidan did in the new town was find the library, because the house was still boxes and his mother kept saying "we'll acclimate" like it was a science experiment, and the school wouldn't start for nine more days. The library was a squat brick building with a leaking gutter, and inside it smelled like radiator dust and old paper. He chose a table near the window, third from the back, because it had a good view of the door and nobody's coat on the chair.

He went back the next afternoon, and the one after that. On the fourth day he texted Sawyer: found a spot, same table every day, it's a thing now. Sawyer replied with a thumbs up and a photo of the old group at the diner, the booth by the jukebox, six shoulders crammed together, and Aidan stared at it long enough that the screen dimmed.

On the fifth day someone was sitting at his table. A girl his age with a biology textbook open to a chapter on cellular respiration, chewing the cap of a highlighter. He stood there holding his book until she looked up.

"Sorry, is this yours?"

"I mean, no," Aidan said. "It's the library's."

She laughed at that, which he hadn't intended but decided to accept. She said her name was Leyla, that she came here after cross-country practice because her house had four younger cousins in it and the coffee shop on Miller Street charged for wifi. He sat down across from her instead of finding another table, which surprised him a little.

They fell into it slowly, over six or seven afternoons. She was pugnacious about almost everything, which he learned meant she argued the way other people said hello. She argued that the library's fine system was punitive, that the new crossing light on Chestnut was a waste of tax money, that anyone who dog-eared pages instead of using a bookmark was a menace to civilization. He argued back, carefully at first, testing whether she wanted a real opponent or an audience. She wanted an opponent.

It was her, not any adult, who gave him the word. He'd been trying to explain why he kept coming to this same scratched table, why it mattered more than it should, and she waved her highlighter at him. "Haven't you ever heard of third places? Sociologist Ray Oldenburg. He wrote this book in 1989, The Great Good Place. He called them third places, cafes, libraries, wherever people meet that isn't home and isn't work." She said it like she was telling him the obvious, the way you'd tell someone water was wet, and then went back to her diagrams.

Aidan wrote the phrase in the margin of his notebook that night and sat with it. He had thought he was hiding, or waiting, or being pathetic in a dignified way, and here was a man with a book saying that the table was the point, that people had built their whole lives around such tables for as long as there'd been towns. He tested the idea against his own cynicism, which said that no sociology book could make a town with a leaking gutter into a home. But the cynicism had a thin veneer lately, and under it was the fact that he'd memorized the librarian's shifts and the sound the front door made.

When school started, Mr. Kang, who taught his economics class, assigned seats alphabetically and Aidan landed two chairs from Leyla, who mouthed "third place" at him across the room when Mr. Kang said the cafeteria would be closed for renovations in October. That night he texted Sawyer an actual paragraph, not a thumbs up. He wrote: I'm not replacing the booth. The booth's still the booth. But there's a table here too, and it turns out you're allowed to have both, or at least I'm trying it out, I'll let you know. He read it twice, deleted "or at least I'm trying it out," then put it back in, because it was the true version.

Sawyer texted back a photo of the empty booth with a caption: it waits. And on Saturday morning Aidan walked to the library with two coffees in a cardboard carrier, set one in front of Leyla's spot, and watched the door.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: An intersect overlay in GIS keeps only the areas that appear in both input layers, so intersecting housing with a flood zone shows just the homes inside the zone.
story:
The flight to Tucson was delayed twice, and by the second delay Camille had claimed the last seat with an outlet, near a pillar, in Concourse B. She opened her laptop on her knees and looked at the map she had been carrying around for two weeks: her city, whole and green, with every parcel of housing drawn on it, hundreds of small polygons bleeding together at the edges.

Ms. Hoang had assigned the project before spring break. Overlay flood risk and housing, she had said, and tell me who lives where the water goes. Camille had imagined it would take an afternoon. Instead she had spent the break clipping layers, recoloring them, and producing, again and again, the same useless result: a map of every house in the city, whether the river touched it or not.

"You look peevish," said Regan, dropping into the seat across from her with a paper cup of coffee. Regan was on the same flight; they had found each other at the security line, both surprised the other was going to the same college admitted-students day. "Or constipated. One of those."

"I did the overlay wrong." Camille turned the screen so Regan could see. "Ms. Hoang wants only the houses inside the flood zone. I got all of them."

Regan set the coffee down and leaned in. She had taken the advanced section the previous semester, the one with the Saturday labs. "What did you use?"

"The union tool. It looked like the right one."

"That keeps everything from both layers." Regan tapped the edge of the trackpad. "Use the intersect tool instead. An intersect overlay keeps only the areas that appear in both input layers, so intersecting housing with a flood zone shows just the homes inside the zone." She said it fast, the way she recited lab procedures, then pointed at the menu. "There. Third one down."

Camille clicked it. The green mass thinned. The river's hatched flood boundary stayed fixed on the screen, and inside it, where the two layers agreed, a scatter of small shapes remained: a strip of houses along Delacroix Street, a couple of blocks off Ninth, a trailer park she had driven past a hundred times without seeing. Everything else went pale.

"Oh," Camille said. She zoomed in on Delacroix. Thirty-one houses, maybe thirty-five; she would count them properly when she wasn't balancing a laptop on her knees.

"You didn't know that neighborhood flooded?"

"I knew it flooded. I didn't know it was those houses." She had learned the word floodplain in fourth grade, had sandbagged the church basement with her mother in eighth, had watched the news helicopter circle the river every third spring. But the word had never attached itself to addresses. Now it had. She dragged the map south along the river and the shapes kept appearing, block after block, and she thought of how her mother had signed an affidavit that spring for the insurance claim, standing at the kitchen table swearing under penalty of perjury that the water had reached the third stair, and how the adjuster had needed a photograph of the water line to believe them.

At the gate, the agent announced preboarding. A woman with a stroller went first, then a man with a cane. Camille kept working. She began a table beside the map, one row per house, columns for what Ms. Hoang had told them to operationalize: flood risk in one column, housing in the others, age of structure, tenure, assessed value. The word had bothered her when Ms. Hoang first used it, all machinery and no feeling, but she understood it now as a way of making something countable so it could be argued with, the way the affidavit had made the water line into evidence a company would have to accept.

Regan was watching over her cup. "You know the flood maps are old," she said. "Like, they haven't been redrawn since before the levee work. Half those houses might not be in the zone anymore, and other ones might be in it that aren't drawn."

"That's true," Camille said. She looked at the boundary line, its confident hatching, and then at the houses inside it, which were real regardless of the line's age. She added a column to the table and titled it confidence, and in the first row, for the first house on Delacroix, she wrote the word medium.

"So is that the whole project?" Regan asked.

"I don't know yet. Ms. Hoang asked who lives where the water goes. I can show the houses now. The who part I still have to find out." She saved the file twice, the way she had learned to after losing a draft to a dead battery, and closed the laptop as the agent called their group.

They walked toward the scanner together. Regan held her boarding pass up to the blue light and it turned green. Camille followed, and while the machine read her own pass she was still counting in her head, thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three houses, all of them sitting inside that hatched line until she could prove otherwise.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: Landscape architect Ian McHarg's 1969 book Design with Nature promoted stacking maps of soil, water and other factors to decide land use, an idea that GIS later automated.
story:
Lucas had been staring at the same screen for forty minutes, and the map still refused to tell him anything. The software had let him color every property lot in the east end by its flood risk, a tidy gradient from pale yellow to an alarming red, and then he had added the housing data as a second layer, and the two layers sat on top of each other like transparencies on an overhead projector, politely ignoring each other. He could see both. He could not see what they meant together.

"Try making the flood layer forty percent transparent," Tegan said, leaning over from the next station. She smelled like the cafeteria's orange disinfectant, which everyone carried by fourth period.

"I did. Then it's just mud-colored everywhere."

Prince, two seats down, spun his chair. "Mine's worse. I mapped income, and now my city looks like it lost a fight with a highlighter."

Ms. Carvalho moved between the rows without stopping, the way she did, hands clasped behind her like a general inspecting an army that was losing. "The overlay has to reveal a pattern, not just coexist," she said, and passed on before Lucas could ask the obvious question, which was how.

He took the assignment home because there was no choice: identify which neighborhoods faced the highest flood risk and what kind of housing stood there, and defend the method. At his grandfather's apartment that evening, hunting through a closet for a borrowed stapler, he found instead a cardboard tube that had been standing behind the winter coats longer than Lucas had been alive. Inside were maps. Real ones, on thin tracing paper, some penciled, some inked, each sheet showing one thing and one thing only: soil, here; water, here; slopes, here; where the houses were, here.

"What's this stuff?" he asked, carrying the tube into the kitchen.

His grandfather turned a sheet over in his hands. "Planning maps. We did it by hand, back when I worked for the county. Soil on one sheet, water on another, the rest on more, and you stack them on a light table and look through them all at once. There was a book that got everybody doing it. Landscape architect, Ian McHarg. Design with Nature, 1969. He said you stack the maps of the soil and the water and the other factors and let them decide the land use." He shrugged. "Half our office copied him. Slower than anything. You'd sneeze and ruin a week."

Lucas laid the sheets on the kitchen table, one on top of another, and squinted down through them. Where the water sheet and the soil sheet and the slope sheet darkened together, the stack went nearly opaque, and there, underneath, sat the housing sheet with its tight rows of small lots. He didn't need a computer to see it. The low ground near the river, the cheap land, the cheap houses, all gathered in the same dark corner of the stack like they had been assigned there.

Back at school the next morning, he rebuilt his map before Prince had finished complaining about the bus. Flood layer underneath, transparent. Housing layer above, transparent. But this time he gave each layer a job, weighting the flood risk so the dangerous zones bled through the housing symbols instead of hiding under them, and the pattern arrived all at once: the red reached up into the densest blocks of rental housing exactly where the paper stack had gone dark, the river's littoral edge, where the oldest and cheapest streets ran. The neighborhoods that could least afford it stood on the ground most likely to go under.

"Okay, that's actually something," Tegan said, arms crossed, studying it. "So the city should just not have put housing there?"

"That's the thing," Lucas said slowly. "It's not that simple." He had worked it out on the bus, or half worked it out, the two ways of thinking arguing in his head like Prince and Tegan at their worst. The map said the land was wrong for housing. The housing was already there, though, full of people who needed somewhere to live, and a flood map couldn't tell you whether moving them would help or just sequester them in some other bad place nobody had mapped yet. The stack showed you the problem. It didn't show you the answer. His grandfather's old office had drawn those sheets fifty years before the software existed, and the software had made the stacking instant, but it hadn't made the deciding instant, and maybe that was the whole point. The machine automated the maps. It didn't automate the judgment.

When his turn came to present, he put the map on the screen and the old tracing paper on the desk beside it, the actual sheets, which his grandfather had let him take after only one meaningful pause. "These are the same idea, fifty years apart," he said. "McHarg's method, by hand and by software. The digital one just does the stacking automatically." Then he showed the dark corner, the red reaching into the rental blocks, and said, honestly, that he knew what the pattern was and did not know what to do about it, and that anyone who claimed the map alone decided was selling something.

Ms. Carvalho looked at the tracing paper for a long moment before she looked at him. "Where's the flood wall in all this?" she asked. "The existing one."

Lucas stared at his own map, on which he had not, until that second, thought to put it.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: The legal age of consent differs by country and even between US states, and in many places it falls between 16 and 18.
story:
The clinic kept a binder of peer-educator schedules on the reception desk, and Justine found her name there in pencil, slotted for two o'clock, her first afternoon shadowing in the exam rooms. She had volunteered after Ms. Baptiste, who ran the health elective at school, mentioned that the clinic wanted students trained to explain the basics to people their own age. Justine had assumed the training would be a handout and a lanyard. Instead the nurse practitioner slid a laminated card across the counter and said, "Teach it back to me before you see anyone."

Justine stood in the corridor and worked through the card, first consent, then contraception, then how testing worked, what a person asked for at the front desk, how long results took, which tests were swabs and which were blood. Consent was the part she kept restarting. She knew what it meant in her own life, but explaining it aloud made her hear how it could slide into platitude, yes means yes, no means no, sentences that sounded complete and explained nothing. She tried again, slower. Consent was ongoing, she said, and specific, and it couldn't be given by someone asleep or pressured or afraid. The nurse nodded once and pointed her toward the waiting room.

Teagan was there, which Justine had not expected. She sat with her jacket zipped to her chin though the waiting room was warm, and when she saw Justine she looked at the floor, then back up, then said, "Don't. I know you work here now." Justine sat one chair away and said she didn't work anywhere, she was learning. "Learning what," Teagan said, and it came out sharper than a question.

"Consent. Contraception. How to get tested," Justine said, and the words sat in the air between them, doing more than she intended. Teagan's chin dropped. She said she'd looked up the clinic's address four times this week and walked past it twice. She said her mother thought she was at Mohamed's study group.

They went through it in low voices. Justine walked her through the front desk, the form, the part where you could ask for a full panel or just the ones you had reason to worry about, the swab and the blood draw, the wait for results. She named the contraception options she could remember and admitted where her memory ran out, and said the clinic could walk Teagan through the rest better than a card could. Teagan listened with her hands folded, and then, without raising her head, she said, "Is it legal. Me and him. He's nineteen."

Justine started to say of course, then stopped, because she did not actually know. She pulled out her phone and looked it up right there, the screen angled so only they could see it. Sixteen, in their state. She told Teagan that, and Teagan exhaled, and then Mohamed's voice arrived before he did, breathless from the stairs, saying his grandmother had sent him with Teagan's phone charger and also there was a news article he'd read on the bus about a law in another country, some case where a couple's ages made it a crime there, and it had surprised him because it was different from here. "Wait," Teagan said. "It's different in other places?"

Justine scrolled while Mohamed leaned over the back of the chair. It wasn't just countries, she found. Even between US states the age of consent differed, and in many places it fell somewhere between sixteen and eighteen. She said it plainly, the way the screen gave it, and none of them said anything for a moment, the fact rearranging something Teagan had clearly assumed was one fixed line and not a shifting one. Mohamed said, "So it depends where you are," and Justine said, "Yeah," and heard the tectonic weight of that land on Teagan, who had been building her whole panic on the idea that legality was a single number written somewhere permanent.

"Here it's sixteen," Justine said. "Where we are. That's what matters for you today." Teagan nodded, and the nurse called a name from the doorway, and Teagan stood, and unzipped her jacket, and picked up the form the receptionist had left on the seat beside her. Mohamed held out the charger. Teagan looked back at them both and said, "If you're still learning, you can practice on me after."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Molar mass in grams per mole has the same number as a particle's average mass in atomic mass units; one carbon atom averages about 12.01 units, and one mole of carbon about 12.01 grams.
story:
Clara arrived early to the lab because her first attempt at the homework had produced a mass of sodium chloride large enough to season a small nation, and Mr. Costa had written one word beside it in red: "units?" She sat at the bench near the window, the one with the fume hood that never quite stopped humming, and spread out her periodic table, her calculator, and the worksheet that asked her to find the moles of product formed from a given mass of reactant. The reactant was 5.00 grams of carbon, which was supposed to react with excess chlorine gas, and she was supposed to get from grams to moles to something sensible at the end.

Zak dropped into the seat across from her, spinning a pencil between his fingers. "Did you get number four?" he asked. "Because I got number four and I don't believe it."

"I got a number," Clara said. "I don't believe mine either."

The problem was the ladder, as Mr. Costa called it. Grams of reactant became moles of reactant, moles of reactant became moles of product through the balanced equation, and moles of product became whatever you wanted at the end. Clara could see the ladder. What she could not see was the rung in the middle, the conversion itself, the place where grams turned into moles. On her first attempt she had divided by the atomic number instead of the molar mass, or multiplied when she should have divided, and the answer had ballooned into absurdity.

She stared at the periodic table. Carbon's little box held the number 6 at the top and 12.01 in the fractional light beneath the symbol. She had used the 6. That was the mistake. You divided by the 12.01, the other number, the heavier-looking one that sat lower in the box. She wrote it out: 5.00 grams of carbon, divided by 12.01 grams per mole, which gave her 0.416 moles of carbon. Then the equation said one mole of carbon made one mole of the product, so 0.416 moles it was. The answer was smaller than the starting mass, which felt right for the first time all week.

"But why 12.01?" she said aloud, mostly to the periodic table. "Why that number and not some other one?"

Zak leaned over. "That's the atomic mass. Average mass of one atom. It's in units, though, not grams. Atomic mass units." He tapped the box. "Little tiny units for little tiny atoms."

Clara wrote 12.01 twice on her scratch paper, once with "one atom, about 12.01 atomic mass units" beside it, and once with "one mole, 12.01 grams" beside it. She looked at the two lines for a long moment. The same number. Not similar numbers, not coincidentally close numbers, but the same number doing double duty, describing one atom and also describing 6.02 times ten to the twenty-third of them. It was as if the universe had decided that a single atom's average mass, measured in atomic mass units, and a whole mole's mass, measured in grams, should wear identical faces. She felt something tectonic shift in her understanding, a slow grinding rearrangement of what she had assumed the table meant. "One carbon atom averages about 12.01 units," she said slowly, "and one mole of carbon is about 12.01 grams. The same number. It works both ways."

"Sure," Zak said. "That's how it works."

"But that's strange," Clara said. "That's genuinely strange. It means the table is telling you two things at once and you have to know which question you're asking." She wondered, not for the first time that week, whether the strangeness was in the world or only in her habit of half-reading it.

Mr. Costa came around the benches collecting the homework, and when he reached Clara's paper he paused on her second attempt. "Better," he said. "Now, one gram of carbon. How many moles? In your head."

Clara ran it without writing. One gram divided by 12.01 grams per mole, so a little less than a twelfth of a mole, roughly 0.083. "A twelfth," she said. "About. One over 12.01."

From the back, Skye, who had spent the period defending her own answer with increasing volume, said, "That's sophistry. You can't just say a twelfth when the number is 12.01."

"It's an estimate," Clara said. "The exact number is 0.0832. I'm allowed to notice it's close to a twelfth."

Mr. Costa smiled at that and moved on, and Clara turned back to her scratch paper, where the two 12.01s still sat side by side. She had spent the whole unit treating stoichiometry as a set of procedures to memorize, a ritual of dividing and multiplying in the sanctioned order, and she was starting to suspect she'd been historicizing it all wrong, filing it under "things invented to torment students" when it belonged under "things people discovered because they needed to count atoms they could never see." She could not yet say why the same number worked for one atom and for a mole. That part stayed dark, a door she could see the shape of but not open. She wrote a question mark next to it, an honest mark, and then beneath it: 5.00 g carbon gives 0.416 mol product, check against class.

Zak read it upside down. "You're keeping the question mark?"

"I'm keeping the question mark," Clara said, and boxed the answer.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US National Labor Relations Act, signed on July 5, 1935, gave most private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively.
story:
John had taken the warehouse job because the pay was four dollars an hour above the grocery store where his friend Mederick worked, and because his mother had said the summer would be long. His first week he learned the shape of the place: the loading docks that breathed heat at noon, the forklifts backing up with their insistent beeping, the aisle of noxious solvents near the paint station where you had to watch your eyes. He was sixteen, the youngest on the floor by a decade, and the older workers treated him with a dry, teasing kindness, telling him to lift with his legs and not to trust the ladder by bay nine.

His problem began on a Thursday, when he counted his hours and found that eleven of them were missing from his stub. He had kept his own tally in the back of a school notebook, because Ms. Janssen, his history teacher, had inculcated in him the habit of writing things down, dates especially, and the tally said sixty-one hours while the stub said fifty. When he asked the shift supervisor, the man looked at the paper, then at John, and said the system rounded shifts down and there was nothing to do about it, and then he said the word "temporary" in a way that made it clear the word applied to John.

Mederick worked across town at the grocery store, and on Friday they sat on the hood of Mederick's brother's car eating gas station sandwiches. Mederick had his own want, which was to save enough by September for a used laptop for his first year of college, and his hours kept getting cut, four days a week down to three, and the manager never said why. "My uncle keeps saying we should organize," Mederick said, picking at the bread. "But some guy at work said it's illegal, like they can fire you just for talking about it."

That Saturday, John went to the public library and asked the reference librarian for books on labor law, feeling vaguely foolish, like a character in one of Ms. Janssen's primary sources. What he found stopped him at a table by the window for a long time. The National Labor Relations Act, signed on July 5, 1935, gave most private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively. He read the sentence twice, then copied it into his notebook, because it had the specific gravity of something that could be used. He called Mederick from the lobby phone. "It's a law," he said. "Nineteen thirty-five. Most private-sector workers. We're not illegal, we're the opposite of illegal."

But when he brought it up in the warehouse break room on Monday, the reaction was not what he expected. Rosa, who had worked the paint station for nine years, said quietly that she had two kids and a job was not a theory, and that in her experience people who talked like that disappeared from the schedule. John felt the truth of it land in him, a weight he had not carried into the room. The law was one thing; the fear was another, and the fear was not irrational. He offered Rosa the rest of his coffee without thinking about it, and she took it, and for a moment neither of them said anything, and that silence felt more honest than his peroration at the table had felt, however correct the date.

He tried a different way. He photocopied the page from the book, the one with the act and its date, and left copies folded in his locker and in his pocket, and he started small, with Omar, a classmate who had just been hired for the summer and whose hours had also been shaved. He showed Omar the stub and the notebook and the photocopied page. "If we compare notes," he said, "maybe we can show them a pattern instead of a complaint." Omar, who wanted badly to be taken seriously as a worker and not as a kid, agreed, and the two of them spent their lunch hour matching entries, and found that every worker under twenty-one had the same eleven hours missing.

They asked for a meeting with the floor manager, all four of the youngest workers together, and John laid the pages on the desk without a speech, just the numbers lined up in columns. The manager looked at the columns for a long moment, then at John, then he said the payroll software would be corrected by the next cycle and that no one was in any trouble, though he said it as though the words had to be pried out, and he did not meet anyone's eyes when he said the word "cycle."

Walking out through the loading dock at dusk, John understood that he did not know whether the law had won anything or whether the manager had simply decided four teenagers with matching notebooks were more trouble than eleven hours. Rosa was waiting near the fence, and she said she had heard about the meeting, and she asked, in a voice careful as a held breath, whether the law really was from 1935, and whether it really said workers could bargain. John took the folded photocopy out of his pocket and held it out to her, and Rosa read it under the security light by the fence, moving her lips slightly over the words, "signed on July 5, 1935," while a truck backed slowly in behind them, beeping all the way.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: GIS data comes in two main forms: vector data uses points, lines and polygons, while raster data is a grid of cells, each holding one value.
story:
Raphael's grandfather had converted the back bedroom into a study sometime in the eighties, and the desk still held a rotary pencil sharpener bolted to its edge, but the laptop was new, and the wifi reached the porch, and that was all he needed. He had until Monday to turn in the flood project for Mr. Hoang's class: a map of the east side of the city showing which neighbourhoods sat inside the hundred-year floodplain. Mr. Hoang had offered the topic almost carelessly, one line on a list of options, but Raphael had chosen it because his grandmother's old street had gone under twice in the last decade, and because nobody at school talked about that part of town unless a house there came up cheap.

The trouble began with the data itself. He had downloaded two files from the city's open data portal, a flood map and a housing map, and when he loaded them into the mapping software on his grandfather's desk, they refused to sit together. The housing layer looked like shapes, clean outlines of parcels and buildings, each one you clicked on opening a little table of facts: year built, value, units. The flood layer looked like pixels, a grainy wash of blue laid over the city like weather in an old photograph. He toggled them on and off, dragged their order in the list, restarted the program twice, and the mismatch stayed.

Braden came over on Saturday morning with two energy drinks and no plan to leave. He leaned over Raphael's shoulder with the unselfconscious confidence of someone who has never once lost a file. "It's broken," Braden said. "Just screenshot it and write about the screenshot."

"It's not broken. Look, the shapes work. I can click any house." Raphael selected a parcel near his grandmother's old church and the table popped up instantly. But when he tried the same on the flood layer, nothing. The whole blue wash was one flat thing, no borders, no clicking, no table.

Wade arrived after lunch, having read the assignment sheet on the bus, which was unusual for Wade. He dropped into the wicker chair by the window and watched the screen for a long moment, circumspect in the way he got when he suspected the answer was simpler than anyone wanted it to be. "The shapes," he said. "Those are vector. Vector data uses points, lines and polygons." He pointed at the grainy wash. "That's raster. A grid of cells, each holding one value."

Raphael sat back. The words sorted something in his head, two drawers he hadn't known were separate. The parcels were drawn, like a diagram; the flood layer was photographed in a sense, or built like a photograph, cell by cell. He tried clicking the blue again, then changed tactics. If the raster held one value per cell, then the value was the flood depth, or the risk score, and he didn't need to click anything. He needed to colour the cells, or count the houses that fell on high-value cells.

"So how do I get them to talk to each other?" he asked. Wade shrugged toward the help menu. The afternoon went to trial and error. Raphael found a tool that let him sample the raster at each building polygon, and suddenly the parcel tables had a new column, quiet and numerical, the flood value pulled out of the grid and attached to each shape. It felt less like an answer than a translation. He said so, and Braden laughed at him, but Wade nodded like it mattered.

By evening the map was legible. The houses shaded from pale to dark blue along a line that followed the river's undulate course through the east side, and the pattern was not subtle. His grandmother's old street sat in the deepest colour, dense with dark little polygons, and the hill neighbourhoods to the north held almost none. He printed a draft on the grandfather's ancient printer, its noise carrying through the house, and brought it to the kitchen where his grandfather was soaking beans.

His grandfather put on his glasses and studied the page for a long time, turning it once as if the paper itself might explain. "There's Delgado Street," he said finally, tapping the densest patch. "Your grandmother taught half that block to swim." He said it lightly, but he kept the map, propping it against the fruit bowl, and at dinner he asked Raphael whether the city had seen it, whether anyone with a budget had seen it.

That was the question Raphael couldn't answer by Monday and maybe not after. He knew what the map showed; he did not know whether showing was the same as mattering, and he was circumspect enough now, after a day of nearly writing off working data as broken, not to assume it. What he had was a method. Overlay the shapes on the grid, let each form of data say the thing it was built to say, and see what the comparison surfaced. On Sunday night he added one more layer, a draft of the city's proposed levee extension, a thin polygon drawn straight as a ruler across the meander of the risk. The levee protected the parcels on one side and none on the other. He sat with that a while, the desk lamp humming, his grandfather watching television two rooms away.

He saved the project twice, once to the laptop and once to a stick he'd put in his pocket, and typed the title at the top of the writeup. Under "further questions," where most of the class would write one sentence, he wrote three. Then he went to find his grandfather and show him where the new line was drawn.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by delaying ovulation, and they are more effective the sooner they are taken after unprotected sex.
story:
On the third Tuesday of counselor training, Mr. Menon handed out index cards and told them to write the word "consent" without using the word "yes." Rosalie stared at her card for a long time. Around her, the arts-and-crafts cabin smelled of glue and lake water, and Lucius, two seats over, was already scribbling like the answer had personally insulted him. He tore up two attempts. The whole peer-health program was like this: Mr. Menon refused to tell them anything outright, only asked questions and folded his arms, which Rosalie found equal parts mesmerizing and maddening. She wanted the right answer, and he kept insisting there was a whole ecosystem of them.

"You're overcomplicating it," Lucius whispered, leaning across the gap between their picnic tables. "Just write 'a freely given, reversible, enthusiastic thing that can be withdrawn at any point, including the middle.'" He held up his card like a quiz champion. "That's not even using yes. That's using no, which is basically its opposite, which is basically cheating."

"It's not cheating, it's physics," Rosalie said. "Like enthalpy. The whole is different from the parts." This was a joke, or half of one; she'd taken chemistry the year before and liked the word too much to let it go. Lucius rolled his eyes, but Cade, on her other side, was watching them both with the sullen look he got when he thought a conversation was going somewhere he couldn't follow. Mr. Menon moved through the room collecting cards, and when he reached theirs he read Lucius's answer aloud, and half the cabin laughed, and someone shouted "withdrawable!" like it was a prize on a game show. Rosalie wrote nothing. She was thinking that she could recite definitions all day and still not know what she'd actually say if a real person asked her a real question.

The real question came on Thursday, at the canteen, from a girl named only as the girl from the waterfront cabin, whom everyone called Paddle because of an incident involving a canoe and a wager. Paddle found Rosalie sorting the first-aid supplies and stood in the doorway with her hands jammed in her hoodie pocket. "You're doing the health thing," she said. "The peer thing. Is that, like, a real thing, or a poster thing?"

"It's a real thing," Rosalie said, and waited. Paddle told her, in a rush, staring at the shelf of bandages, that she'd gone into town with a boy from the sailing staff on her night off, and the condom had broken, and that had been Tuesday, and it was Thursday now, and she had not slept since.

Rosalie felt the index-card questions slide off her like water off the dock. Here was the concrete thing, and she had two conflicting instincts at once: one said this is exactly what the training was for, and the other said you are sixteen and you don't know anything yet, find an adult. She had learned that both instincts could be true at once. "Okay," she said. "Is the pharmacy in town open? The one by the hardware store?"

From Lucius's point of view, the whole afternoon looked like this: Rosalie materializing at the sail shed, demanding his bike, refusing to explain, then explaining in one breathless sentence, and then Paddle appearing behind her with her hood up despite the heat. He had a first-aid kit, a whistle, a laminated safety certification, and, apparently, the only functioning bicycle at camp. He also had, he realized as he pedaled the three of them the two miles into town with Paddle riding the handlebars of the borrowed maintenance bike, absolutely no idea what emergency contraception actually was or did. He'd assumed it was a thing that happened at hospitals, with forms.

The pharmacist was a small, brisk woman in reading glasses who took one look at the three of them, hot and dust-striped, and asked what she could help with. Paddle managed the sentence. The pharmacist nodded, reached for a box, and said, matter-of-factly, "The sooner you take it, the better. It works mainly by delaying ovulation, and it's more effective the closer to the event." She glanced at Paddle. "Tuesday, you said? So you'll want to take it today. Waiting a few days would be a mistake." She rang it up, mentioned the price, mentioned that Paddle could ask the clinic in the next town about testing anytime, no appointment drama, and slid the bag across the counter like it was a box of cough drops, which, Lucius thought, was maybe the kindest thing anyone had done all week.

They sat on the curb outside the hardware store while Paddle read the insert in the box. "It says it won't end a pregnancy that's already started," she said. "So it's not what I was scared it was." She swallowed the pill with warm water from a bottle, made a face, and then, for the first time all afternoon, laughed, a short surprised sound. Rosalie laughed too. Lucius said, "For the record, I thought it involved a form. Like a permissions form. At a hospital. Possibly notarized." Paddle threw a gravel at him, gently.

On the ride back, Rosalie coasted down the long hill with her hands off the bars, which was against every rule Mr. Menon had ever posted. She still didn't have her index-card definition of consent. She had a friend who'd asked a real question and gotten a real answer, and a pharmacist's flat certainty that time mattered, and a worry she could not shake that some future version of this would not go this smoothly. Both things sat in her at once, unreconciled. She decided, provisionally, that this was fine. At the top of the last rise, Paddle stood up on her pedals and shouted into the wind, "Race you to the flagpole."
